title: LG Energy Solution reports progress in LMR batteries - electrive.com
content:
LG Energy Solution and Seoul National University have developed an approach to stabilise LMR batteries. In tests, large-format cells demonstrated improved cycle stability as a result.
LMR battery cell by LG Energy Solution at the InterBattery 2026 battery trade fair.
Image: LG Energy Solutions
The research team investigated gas formation and capacity loss in the cells before adjusting their operating conditions and formation process. The findings have been published in the scientific journal
Nature Communications
LMR cathodes primarily rely on manganese and do not require cobalt. Alongside transition metals such as nickel and manganese, oxygen also participates in the energy-storage process. LG Energy Solution expects this combination to enable high energy density at potentially lower material costs. However, if oxygen oxidised during charging does not fully return to its original state during discharge, it can damage the cell structure and generate gases. In large-format cells, this can increase internal pressure and impair performance.
The research team therefore examined different charging and discharging voltages. According to LG Energy Solution, the recovery of oxidised oxygen increased from 86 to 97 per cent when the upper charge cut-off voltage was reduced from 4.6 to 4.3 volts. Lowering the discharge cut-off voltage from 3.0 to 2.0 volts also returned the oxygen almost completely to its original state.
LMR technology for large-format cells
Based on these findings, LG Energy Solution adjusted the voltage range and formation process for 40-Ah-class LMR cells. Among other measures, a lower temperature was used during formation to reduce gas formation. According to the battery manufacturer, the optimised cells retained 92.2 per cent of their original energy after 883 charge and discharge cycles.
These results demonstrate performance under the selected test conditions. However, LG Energy Solution has not provided details on energy density, charging power or a direct comparison with current production battery chemistries in its announcement. The company has also not disclosed a timeline for series production or specific vehicle projects.
The further development of new cell chemistries is also relevant for LG Energy Solution amid increasing
competition in the battery market
. Although the South Korean manufacturer remained the world’s third-largest battery supplier for electric and hybrid vehicles in the first half of 2026, its market share fell from 9.6 to 8.6 per cent, according to SNE Research. CATL and BYD together already accounted for 54.3 per cent.
LMR could be particularly interesting for LG Energy Solution in the long term because of its high manganese content. The newly published research addresses gas formation, one of the obstacles to using LMR in large-format cells. However, the findings do not yet indicate imminent commercialisation.

title: End after 700 e-buses: Bolloré pulls the plug on Bluebus - electrive.com
content:
Commercial Vehicles
French conglomerate Bolloré has decided to discontinue electric bus production at its subsidiary Bluebus. According to Bolloré, Bluebus never achieved the necessary scale to compete seriously with established manufacturers. At the same time, the activities of battery division Blue Solutions are being realigned.
Bluebus in the 12-meter version
Image: Bluebus
The battery-electric bus manufacturer Bluebus, known primarily among industry specialists in Germany, is ceasing operations and will no longer produce vehicles. This marks the end of what initially appeared to be a success story, 15 years after the company was founded in 2011. During that time, Bluebus delivered nearly 700 electric buses in six- and 12-metre versions to around 60 public transport operators – almost all in France, with the exception of
MIVB/STIB in Brussels
The most important orders came from
Paris-based RATP
– and these later became a major setback for Bluebus. After one of the buses caught fire for the second time within a month in spring 2022, RATP temporarily
grounded all 149 Bluebus vehicles in its fleet
. Together with units delivered later, this meant that 232 Bluebus buses ordered by RATP remained out of service for an extended period. It was not until 2024 that RATP
resumed operations
with the electric buses, ahead of the Olympic Games in Paris.
Faulty insulation caused the fires
Lengthy investigations into the incidents eventually identified short circuits caused by improperly installed insulation in the buses’ batteries as the root cause of the fires. This dealt a severe blow to Bluebus and the wider Bolloré Group, particularly because the batteries had previously been a key selling point of the buses. They were developed and produced in-house by sister company Blue Solutions and used a distinctive solid-state lithium-metal polymer (LMP) technology.
The Bluebus buses were intended to serve as a showcase for this battery technology. However, following the two fires and the findings of the investigation, the reputation of both Bluebus and Blue Solutions suffered, making it more difficult to secure new orders.
Bluebus failed to achieve the necessary scale
Although Bolloré does not explicitly mention the incidents in its latest announcement, they may have contributed to the difficulties facing Bluebus. The group cites a lack of scale as the reason for ending the business: Bluebus never reached the volume required to compete effectively with other manufacturers.
Bluebus is now halting electric bus production, resulting in 74 job losses. A small team will remain to handle maintenance for the approximately 700 vehicles already delivered. Bolloré also intends to sell the research and development division, which employs 17 people, to a European company active in public transport. The deal is reportedly nearing completion.
Future for battery division Blue Solutions
While the bus business is being discontinued due to a lack of economies of scale, Bolloré plans to continue operating its battery division, Blue Solutions, with a focus on developing the upcoming fourth generation (Gen4). These solid-state cells
are designed to operate at room temperature
, with the company targeting ultra-fast charging times of less than 20 minutes, 40 per cent greater range and a high level of safety.
Blue Solutions is targeting vehicle manufacturers with the technology and aims to establish a gigafactory for the cells by 2029. To fund the capital-intensive project, the company is currently seeking a strategic investor.

title: What Really Happens to Spent EV Batteries?
content:
Battery Recycling
EV Batteries
Lithium-Ion Batteries
Battery Manufacturing
Industry Trends
Discover how circular battery recycling transforms retired EV batteries and production scrap into valuable materials, driving sustainability and resilience.
September 8, 2026
6 Min Read
Display of reclaimed materials/elements, including black mass from recycled EV Lithium batteries.
John Keeble / Contributor/Getty Images Europe
Electric vehicles (EVs) are central to global decarbonization efforts, but the energy transition's success depends on more than simply putting more EVs on the road. As battery demand continues to grow, the industry must also consider what happens when millions of batteries eventually reach the end of their automotive life.
The first generations of mass-market EVs are beginning to retire, creating a growing stream of batteries that still contain substantial quantities of valuable materials. How these batteries are managed will influence not only waste reduction and emissions but also the long-term resilience of
battery supply chains
Many assume that once a battery is removed from a vehicle, it becomes waste. But in reality, it is often the beginning of a new phase in the battery lifecycle.
Retired EV batteries are only part of the story. As new cell and battery plants come online, they also generate large volumes of production scrap, from electrode trim and off-specification cells to entire modules, all of which must be recovered for full circularity.
Related:
7 Battery Recycling Companies Scaling Up in North America in 2026
End of life doesn't mean end of value
Research from the World Resources Institute (WRI) shows many batteries are removed from vehicles, with around 70-80% of their original capacity remaining. They continue to function but no longer deliver the level of performance required for long-range automotive applications.
As batteries age through charging cycles, heat exposure and normal chemical degradation, their ability to store and deliver energy gradually declines, and they are unable to meet the high standards vehicle manufacturers require for range, power and reliability.
Once a battery is no longer suitable for automotive use, either it is repurposed for less demanding "
second-life" applications
or it enters the recycling stream, which enables valuable materials to be recovered and returned to manufacturing supply chains. In the near term, manufacturing scrap is the larger stream. New cell plants typically scrap 15 to 30% of output in their early years, and industry analysts expect production scrap to remain the primary feedstock for battery recycling until around 2030, when retired EV volumes begin to overtake it.
Porsche has been repurposing used EV batteries to help power Its Liepzig plant since 2024. Credit: Porsche
However, recovering materials from spent batteries is not always straightforward. While considerable attention has focused on materials such as lithium, nickel, and cobalt, graphite has historically received far less attention.
Graphite is one of the largest material components in modern lithium-ion batteries, serving as the primary anode material and playing an essential role in battery performance, safety and lifespan. It accounts for around 30% of a lithium-ion battery's weight. An average EV equipped with an 80-kWh battery contains close to 80 kilograms of graphite, more than the weight of an average adult.
Related:
DOE Announces Lithium-Ion Recycling Prize Winners
Yet unlike higher-value battery metals, graphite has traditionally been overlooked within recycling systems due to technical challenges and perceptions around its economic value. As a result, much of the graphite contained within battery production scrap and end-of-life batteries has historically been lost during processing, incinerated, releasing significant amounts of carbon into the atmosphere, or sent to landfill rather than returned to the battery supply chain. Anode electrode fabrication alone discards roughly 5 to 15% of coated foil as graphite-rich scrap, much of which is currently lost rather than recovered.
This represents a missed opportunity. By 2030, it is estimated that more than 260,000 tonnes of graphite could be available for recycling each year, representing a market opportunity worth approximately $2.6 billion. Recovering and reusing this material will be increasingly important as battery production scales and demand for critical battery materials continues to rise.
Related:
Why graphite recovery matters
As demand for EVs, grid-scale storage, and other battery-powered technologies continues to grow, improving the recovery of all battery materials will be vital.
Traditionally, graphite production has relied on either natural graphite extraction, which requires mining and extensive purification, or synthetic graphite produced from petroleum-based feedstocks using energy-intensive, high-temperature processes. Both routes carry significant environmental impacts, driving growing interest in recovering graphite from battery production waste and end-of-life batteries.
Recent advances in graphite recovery and regeneration technologies are helping expand the range of battery materials that can be economically recovered and reused. For example,
Orbia Fluor & Energy Materials
(Orbia) has developed a proprietary process to recover and purify graphite from domestic sources, transforming material from battery production scrap and end-of-life batteries into high-purity, battery-grade graphite suitable for future applications.
The same approach can be deployed as a modular unit at the end of an anode coating line, recovering more than 95% of the graphite in scrap and returning it directly to electrode production.
The environmental benefits are significant. Initial analysis indicates that regenerated graphite can reduce CO₂ emissions by up to 70% compared with conventional graphite production pathways. By retaining carbon materials already in circulation, graphite recovery can help lower the environmental footprint of battery manufacturing while reducing reliance on newly extracted resources.
To accelerate commercialization, Orbia is developing a fully circular model by working directly with major OEMs and cell producers, helping achieve net-zero targets whilst remaining economically viable.
While no single technology will solve every challenge associated with battery recycling, improvements in graphite recovery illustrate how innovation is expanding the scope of what can be economically and sustainably recovered from spent batteries.
Recycled graphite attached to air bubbles and rising to the surface of the flotation cell at the graphite recycling system. JENS SCHLUETER / Contributor/AFP.
Strengthening future battery supply chains
The importance of graphite recovery extends beyond sustainability. Today, the global battery industry remains heavily reliant on China for battery-grade graphite production and processing, creating significant supply-chain risks for manufacturers as battery demand continues to grow.
This highlights the need for alternative and more resilient supply chains for critical battery materials. For the UK, Europe, and the US, building domestic battery recycling and material processing capacity will help recover valuable materials already in circulation, reducing dependence on imported resources while strengthening regional manufacturing capabilities.
A circular supply of battery materials can also help manufacturers respond to growing sustainability requirements, regional-content expectations and supply-chain challenges.
Rather than viewing retired batteries as waste, the industry should recognize them as a strategic source of future battery materials. Recovering and reintroducing graphite into the battery value chain can help address both the growing supply-demand gap and the need for more secure, localized sources of critical raw materials.
The future is circular
The future of battery sustainability will be determined not only by how batteries are manufactured, but by how effectively the industry can recover, regenerate and reuse the materials they contain. The industry must move towards a more circular model in which batteries are no longer seen as disposable products, but as long-term reservoirs of strategic materials.
As recycling technologies advance, the focus will increasingly shift from simply managing battery waste to maximizing material recovery, reducing emissions and strengthening supply-chain resilience.
The batteries powering today's vehicles can become the raw materials for tomorrow's, helping create a more sustainable, resilient and locally secure foundation for the energy transition.
True circularity means closing the loop on both retired batteries and the production scrap generated as manufacturing scales, so that no valuable material is lost at either end of the battery's life.
About the Author
John Jaddou
Global Director, New Business Development, Orbia Fluor & Energy Materials
John leads the development of new businesses focused on next-generation battery materials and circular supply solutions, drawing on experience across automotive engineering, advanced materials and strategic business development.

title: Fail-Safe BESS Prevents Thermal Runaway | Viridi Technology
content:
Stationary Batteries
Testing & Safety
Battery News
Interviews
Viridi's anti-propagation architecture is scaling across wastewater infrastructure, commercial sites, and DOE research facilities nationwide.
September 8, 2026
7 Min Read
Viridi battery system at the North Creek pumping station in Pennsylvania.
At a Glance
Viridi's anti-propagation technology prevents thermal runaway from spreading beyond a single battery cell
Systems deliver 32-90 hours of backup power, replacing diesel generators at wastewater and commercial sites
Technology validated by Oak Ridge National Laboratory and deployed at 100 locations across the United States
When a lithium-ion battery cell enters
thermal runaway
, it typically triggers a dangerous domino effect—heat and fire spreading from cell to cell, releasing toxic smoke and gas. But a Buffalo-based company has developed battery energy storage systems (BESS) that arrest failure at a single cell, preventing propagation entirely.
's fail-safe technology is now deployed at nearly 100 sites nationwide, from municipal wastewater pumping stations to Department of Energy research facilities, replacing diesel generators with backup power that delivers up to 90 hours of operation without fuel, emissions, or the safety risks traditionally associated with lithium-ion batteries.
"Fail-safe" is not a concept that Jon M. Williams discusses in uncertain terms. He's deliberate about it. He's specific to the point that there can be no delineation between what does and does not qualify as such. So when he characterizes the nature of his company's battery energy storage system (BESS) as "fail-safe," he truly means that the pack has been developed to remain safe in the event of a failure. And make no mistake about it — as with any battery, any cell, any base for stored energy — the potential for failure will always be there. And if a failure occurs there will be a release of energy that requires proper mitigation to uphold this high level of safety.
Related:
How AI is Driving the Fastest Shift in Stationary Battery Applications in Decades
"A cell is going to fail and fail without us knowing about it at some point," said Williams, chief executive officer at Viridi, a startup organization based in Buffalo, NY, that designs and manufactures lithium-ion BESS units and battery-powered industrial equipment. "And when this happens you have to prevent that unplanned release of energy from spreading to another cell and lighting that on fire."
Viridi CEO Jn M. Williams. Credit: Viridi
This approach has led to the development of a unique BESS architecture that arrests battery cell failure at a single cell, preventing propagation. This core technology has continued to evolve into successful deployments throughout a variety of settings, including in the past year alone at a municipal wastewater pumping station, a grid research innovation and development center, and numerous commercial sites managed by reportedly the fastest-growing energy-as-a-service (EaaS) company in the United States.
UL testing sets new safety standard
Launched in 2018 when the company's first round of investors was welcomed, Viridi was established on the basis of proving that anti-propagation technology could prevent the dangerous chain-of-event reactions associated with the spreading of heat and fire that lithium-ion battery packs have been associated with, which Williams said required testing through Underwriters Laboratories (UL) that had not been conducted previously per the company's fail-safe standard.
Related:
NeoVolta, SK On Announce One of Largest Domestic Battery Deals Since OBBBA Passage
The company tested to a slab-mount residential standard unprecedented in the industry, with no detectable smoke, gas, or flame. The organization's first indoor installation occurred in 2020 at a medical campus in Buffalo with a 600-kilowatt-hour (kWh) system located inside a medical research building.
Opportunity not to waste
This same pack design — the
— is also being utilized at the sewer wastewater station in Erie County, PA, a project that officials in the city of Hamburg credit with strengthening the region's public infrastructure, reducing operational costs and diesel emissions, and demonstrating how clean energy can replace traditional backup power at scale. Viridi's solution was sought when one of the county's lift stations became compromised after a diesel generator aged-out and power proved unreliable.
"By replacing the outdated diesel generator with a Viridi battery energy storage system, we eliminate fuel dependency, expect reductions in maintenance costs, and achieve near-instant backup power," said Angela M. Horton, P.E., senior sanitary engineer at Erie County's division of sewerage management. "This transition not only cuts our emissions, but we expect improvements in reliability and resilience for these critical wastewater pumping operations — and it dovetails neatly with Erie County's ongoing climate and energy goals. While the Viridi system was only recently installed, we are very optimistic about its future impacts."
Related:
Cummins Wins Its Largest BESS Contract for US Data Center Project
Exterior of the North Creek pump station in Erie County, PA. Credit: Viridi
Real-world performance: 32-90 hours of backup power
The 150-kWh system delivers 32-90 hours of backup power, depending on pump demand, and ensures continuous operation through outages without the fuel consumption, emissions, or maintenance burdens typical of the diesel system, said Williams. Diesel generators can cost up to $10,000 annually for upkeep.
With real-time remote monitoring and alerts, the BESS also reduces truck rolls, enables immediate detection of system issues, and enhances overall reliability for wastewater operations, said Williams. With a reported nearly 100 similar pump stations in the area, there could be future opportunities.
"This project shows what's possible when public infrastructure embraces safer, smarter, and more sustainable energy technologies," said Williams. The project could likewise set a new benchmark for how cities deploy battery storage to strengthen infrastructure. Beyond wastewater systems, Viridi also boasts governmental institutions including public libraries, and military academies.
The RPS50 features:
150-kWh capacity
32-90 hours backup power
3,500 cycle life
Real-time remote monitoring via IoT
Modular, scalable configuration
Through Viridi's control technology, the company can upload and download software remotely and fully control the unit and what it's connected to. Anything you can do on the control panel standing in front of the unit can be done remotely through the company's internet of things (IoT) technology.
For lift station purposes, officials can see when pumps turn on and off, real-time power usage for the utility, and when outages occur. "If the system is engaged it sends a signal to the water authority and tells them there's a maintenance issue to address before it fails," said Williams. "It's an energy management system, not just a backup."
Additionally, Viridi is eligible for the Investment Tax Credit, which reportedly brings the county 40 percent of spending back from the federal government.
Nationwide expansion: 100 commercial sites
As the company continues to scale operations, a nationwide deployment initiative announced this summer will reportedly bring Viridi's BESS to 100 commercial sites across the U.S. that are managed by the EaaS group
Budderfly
, Shelton, CT. The collaborative, which will employ Viridi's RPSLinkEX (or exterior) platform will serve commercial sites facing grid constraints and pressure to improve resiliency and sustainability. This effort also marks a significant expansion of Budderfly's energy infrastructure, according to the company.
"This partnership is an important milestone in Budderfly's multi-phase energy storage strategy," said Al Subbloie, chief executive officer. "As electricity demand continues to grow, businesses need integrated energy solutions that help them operate more efficiently while supporting the evolving needs of the grid."
Battery deployments are currently advancing across Massachusetts, Connecticut, and California as part of the first phase of the strategic expansion. Recent installations include commercial and manufacturing sites.
"Together, we're helping customers address growing energy demand challenges while supporting a more resilient energy future," said Williams.
Viridi's RPS 150 battery energy storage system installed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory's (ORNL) Power Distribution Field Test Site. Credit: Viridi.
DOE partnership validates grid-scale technology
In July, Viridi also announced an alliance to support research into next-generation utility grid technologies that advance grid resilience and reliability with
Oak Ridge National Laboratory
(ORNL), a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) national facility. Viridi's BESS was selected and
installed at ORNL's Grid Research Innovation and Development Center (GRID-C)
as part of a testing platform for a DOE resource integration and evaluation project. The system supports research into controlling grid resources to meet utility needs.
"This project bridges an important gap by integrating real electrical equipment to understand realistic performance challenges, proving the robustness of ORNL's new control strategies and AC/DC (alternating current/direct current) architecture for supporting the future grid," said Madhu Sudhan Chinthavali, electrical systems integration program manager at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. "Viridi's battery integrated seamlessly with our management system, and its engineering team supported our researchers throughout testing and integration, making them a valuable partner."
The application is exactly the type of environment that Viridi was intended for, according to Williams. "Being selected by Oak Ridge National Laboratory to support the project is a milestone for Viridi and a validation of what we have built," he said. "When a DOE national lab chooses your technology to support their research, it is the highest bar a battery system can meet."
The collaboration stands as the beginning of an ongoing research relationship between the two entities, with additional joint projects being planned. "Our whole business is to optimize and bring greater efficiency to the existing assets we have for electric generation and distribution," said Williams. "When you do that, you bring down the cost for everybody. You don't have to build more wires and poles. And you add resiliency to every location you put the pack."

Joe Darrah is an award-winning freelance journalist based in the Philadelphia region who covers a variety of topics, including healthcare and medical technology. His articles have been published in more than 40 publications.

title: Advanced Battery Safety and Testing with ARC Technology
content:
Testing & Safety
Thermal Management
Interviews
Learn from Danny Montgomery, Technical Services Manager at Thermal Hazard Technology, about ARC testing for advanced battery safety analysis.
September 8, 2026
6 Min Read
A prismatic cell set up inside the EV+ calorimeter for an overcharge test, with current cables attached.
Thermal Hazard Technology.
This article is part two of a two-part series focusing on battery safety and testing. The first part covered techniques that can uncover fundamental information on battery materials at the research and development phase, the types of abuse tests that cells and battery packs undergo to ensure they’re safe for public use, and how battery management systems (BMS) use sensor data to manage thermal runaway risk.
If you missed the first part, you can find it
. In this second part,
Battery Technology
spoke to Danny Montgomery, Technical Services Manager at
Thermal Hazard Technology
, about using Accelerating Rate Calorimeter (ARC) testing to obtain information about a battery’s safety.
What is ARC testing?
Danny Montgomery, Technical Services Manager at Thermal Hazard Technology:
ARC testing uses an ‘Accelerating Rate Calorimeter’, which is a device that measures heat, to evaluate the safety and performance of batteries. ARC testing is not a ‘pass-or-fail’ type test but is instead a quantitative analysis which can report many different parameters and provide a comprehensive evaluation of cell-level battery safety. It’s a widespread technique in the battery industry and is mostly used in cell development to try and understand how changes to the cell―for example, the chemical formulation―can improve the cell’s safety and performance.
Related:
Battery Safety Testing and Monitoring Methods Explained
18650 cell set up for testing inside standard calorimeter with voltage wires and thermocouples attached. Courtesy of Thermal Hazard Technology.
How is ARC testing performed on cells?
Montgomery:
The cell is placed inside a cylindrical calorimeter chamber, sensors are attached, and the machine runs a pre-programmed heating procedure via the control software. Other tests such as nail penetration or overcharge can also be carried out depending on the auxiliary modules attached to the ARC. A fixture is sometimes used to hold or compress the cell, but this is not mandatory.
The system is quite flexible, so the type of cell and the sensors used can easily be changed from one test to another. The machine allows the pre-programming of test procedures, and running a test involves loading a test file, confirming settings, and pressing start. The cooling and flushing process following the test is also automated. Unfortunately, post-test clean up still requires human intervention.
What information can be obtained using ARC testing?
Montgomery:
At the R&D stage, the ARC helps to refine the chemical composition of the battery and the design of the cell. The safety parameters and performance of different chemical formulations can be easily quantified as the test data is highly repeatable. One of the common metrics obtainable by ARC testing is the onset temperature―the temperature when unfavorable chemical reactions start to rapidly increase the temperature inside the cell prior to thermal runaway―and cell developers are trying to increase this temperature to make the cell more stable at higher temperatures [a higher onset temperature will increase the temperature when thermal runaway starts].
Related:
Strengthening Fire Safety for BESS Containers Through Testing
On production cells, the ARC can be used for quality control. Samples are taken from a batch of cells to check that their thermal behavior matches that of previous batches. This helps ensure there are no problems with the manufacturing process from a safety perspective (not electrical performance).
ARC testing can also evaluate aged cells to determine the safety impact of the aging process. Cells which have been through hundreds of cycles may be less thermally stable and this should be considered when it comes to evaluating the long-term reliability of the battery system.
EV+ calorimeter inside the Extended Blast Enclosure, which safely contains the gas, flame and smoke resulting from thermal runaway testing in the calorimeter. Courtesy of Thermal Hazard Technology.
Is ARC testing used as a standalone technique or is it used as part of a suite of diagnostic platforms?
Montgomery:
ARC can be used as standalone technique. Because it is a system designed to initiate thermal runaway, it is often coupled with devices which analyze gases released by the cell. The ARC can also be used with additional sensors to try and gather more information from the test―an infrared (IR) camera, for example. Postmortem techniques are also useful when combined with ARC testing to try and discover more about the failure mode of the cell.
Related:
EV Battery Safety Through Advanced Testing Techniques
As part of a safety testing lab, the ARC may be accompanied by other test equipment designed to implement specific thermal runaway trigger methods. Cyclers may be used in conjunction with the ARC both for cycling cells prior to testing, or for cycling insider the calorimeter to measure heat release and cell efficiency.
What are some of the limitations of ARC testing?
Montgomery:
ARC testing is generally limited to cell-level. Small modules are possible to test but the ARC technique does work better with single cells, as it tracks a single temperature. In a module, different cells will be at different temperatures which limits the usefulness of the temperature tracking functionality.
Because ARC testing is highly sensitive, it takes longer than some test methods and can take 1-3 days per test. This means sample throughput is relatively low. Finally, different calorimeter models are needed because as a single model doesn’t cover every cell format. For example, the smallest model is great for coin cells, but a different (larger) model is needed for large blade cells.
Blade cell set up for testing inside the EVx calorimeter. Courtesy of Thermal Hazard Technology.
Are there any batteries that ARC testing can't be used on?
Montgomery:
ARC isn’t used on batteries that have an established “safe” battery chemistry, such as lead acid or nickel-metal hydride, because there is no thermal runaway associated with these cells. Other than that, most reactive cells can be tested, but the user should ensure that the cell capacity does not exceed the limitations of the calorimeter or the dimensional limitations of the testing chamber. In lithium-metal solid-state cells, a protective titanium skin must be used with the calorimeter to protect it from the molten lithium which ejects from the cell during thermal runaway.
What does the cutting-edge of ARC testing look like today?
Montgomery:
The recent developments in ARC testing relate to the increased size of the test chamber and the capacity of cells which can be tested. Commercial cells continue to become larger with a higher capacity and energy density, so the calorimeter must be designed to be able to accommodate these test samples. It should be able to withstand repeated blasts from thermal runaway, so the construction must be durable enough to work for many years under extreme conditions of temperature and pressure. Other developments come from the software and control side. We are currently working on making control and analysis software more user-friendly and making instrument calibration a quicker and simpler process.
How are the cutting-edge systems benchmarked against other ARC testing equipment?
Montgomery:
To make ARC testing reliable, accurate and sensitive, the most important consideration is data quality. Building an ARC to successfully test large samples is an engineering challenge in terms of durability, but it is even more difficult to build a large ARC which can still accurately test small samples, or even chemical and component samples. The system must be benchmarked and able to pass standard test criteria for known samples, which ensure their accuracy for heat measurement. Another cutting-edge aspect is the combination of ARC testing with other analysis techniques such as online gas analysis, IR video or rapid data collection.

Building on almost 10 years of writing experience, Liam has covered a wide berth of areas that interface with chemistry, materials science, energy, nanotechnology, and emerging technology developments for media sites, trade magazines and other organizations around the world. Liam has widely covered different battery architectures through news, opinion, Q&A, and feature articles for different industry applications, and also widely reports on other advances in the energy and electrification sectors surrounding EVs, renewables, and the energy grid. title: Trump's Orders Secure Bulk Power System, Critical Minerals
content:
Battery Manufacturing

Trump's orders aim to secure the US bulk power system and protect critical minerals, ensuring energy resilience. Ford Energy supports this initiative with locally assembled battery storage solutions.
September 8, 2026
5 Min Read
US President Donald Trump speaks during a roundtable on the American mining industry in Washington, DC.
Eric Lee / Stringer/Getty Images News
Because of vulnerabilities in the nation’s energy infrastructure and the urgent need to protect critical components such as transformers and battery energy storage systems (BESS), President Donald J. Trump issued
Executive Order 14420
, declaring a national emergency to secure the U.S. bulk power system. Additionally, the administration has taken further steps to address the scarcity of critical minerals and materials, such as black mass and tungsten, which are vital to the energy and defense sectors.
Understanding “bulk-power system electric equipment”
The term “bulk-power system electric equipment” covers critical components used in substations, control rooms, and power-generating stations. These include reactors, capacitors, transformers, inverters, battery storage systems, and uninterruptible power supplies that support critical infrastructure.
It also covers industrial control systems like remote terminal units, programmable logic controllers, and intelligent electronic devices. It also includes associated software, firmware, and remote access capabilities if they pose risks to the system's security. Equipment unrelated to national security concerns or used solely for local energy distribution is excluded, ensuring focus on safeguarding vital infrastructure from foreign threats.
Related:
Why AI and Critical Materials Are Driving the Future of Battery Supply Chains
The context of Executive Order 14420
The bulk-power system is the backbone of the country’s energy infrastructure, providing electricity to support national defense, emergency services, critical infrastructure, and the economy. However, the increasing reliance on foreign-produced equipment has exposed the system to significant risks, including cyberattacks, supply chain disruptions, and potential sabotage.
President Trump stated in the order, “Certain foreign actors are increasingly creating and exploiting vulnerabilities in the United States bulk-power system, which provides the electricity that supports our national defense, vital emergency services, critical infrastructure, and economy.” He further emphasized the growing risks, saying that “the threat to the United States regarding foreign supply of bulk-power system electric equipment has become even more acute.”
Transformers: The heart of the power grid
Transformers are indispensable to the bulk-power system. They regulate voltage levels and are essential for stepping voltage up or down, ensuring a safe and accurate grid operation. The executive order specifically mentions substation transformers and instrument transformers, recognizing their importance in the grid.
Related:
LG Energy Solution North America President on Battery Market Pivot
Many transformers used in the US are imported, and concerns have been raised about the potential for embedded digital backdoors or other security risks. A compromised transformer could disrupt power supply, damage critical infrastructure, and even jeopardize national security. By prioritizing the protection and replacement of foreign-produced transformers, the executive order aims to eliminate these risks and strengthen the power grid's resilience.
Ford is leveraging its existing manufacturing infrastructure by converting its Glendale, Kentucky, battery plant—originally built for EV batteries—into a facility for assembling energy storage systems. Courtesy of Ford.
Battery energy storage systems
The executive order explicitly includes BESS in its definition of bulk-power system electric equipment, stating that it includes “battery energy storage systems; and uninterruptible power supply systems supporting critical infrastructure.” This recognition underscores the growing importance of BESS in the bulk-power system and the need to secure it against potential threats.
The supply chain for BESS components, including lithium-ion batteries, is heavily dependent on foreign sources, raising concerns about potential disruptions. The order empowers the Secretary of Energy to act to “identify, isolate, monitor, secure, disconnect, replace, or remove” foreign-manufactured equipment that poses a risk to national security. Before directing isolation, disconnection, replacement, or removal, the Secretary shall consider effects on reliability and safety, the availability of secure replacements, and continuity of essential services.
Related:
Inside LGES's New $2B Michigan Battery Plant
Ford Energy’s bold move
To align with the goals of Executive Order 14420, Ford Energy has
announced
its commitment to bolstering US energy infrastructure with domestically assembled solutions. The company’s President, Dave Carroll, emphasized Ford’s century-long legacy of serving American needs, stating, “Ford Energy was founded in the spirit of advancing American interests. We are one of very few American companies with the capabilities to deliver U.S.-assembled battery energy storage systems at scale.”
Ford also reiterated that Ford Energy’s LFP prismatic battery energy storage systems will be assembled at
Ford Energy Systems
, a wholly owned and operated gigafactory in Glendale, Kentucky, backed by a bankable brand and a resilient supply chain strategy.
Black mass material ready for processing at Electra’s refinery. Courtesy of Electra.
Addressing critical minerals and materials: Black mass
In addition to securing the bulk-power system, the administration has also taken steps to address
critical mineral
scarcity through the Defense Priorities and Allocations System Directive Allocation Order issued by the
Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)
. This temporary final rule restricts the exportation of
black mass
and tungsten waste and scrap without a license, ensuring that these materials are prioritized for domestic use.
The directive states that “U.S. persons engaged in the sale of black mass and tungsten waste and scrap must allocate 100 percent of monthly sales to U.S. persons, unless an adjustment or exception is obtained in advance from BIS.” This measure, effective from August 27, 2026, to August 27, 2027, is part of a broader effort to secure the supply of recoverable critical minerals and materials essential for national defense and energy resilience.
Black mass, a byproduct of recycling lithium-ion batteries, is a key source of critical minerals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel, which are vital for BESS and other advanced technologies. By restricting its export, the administration aims to bolster domestic manufacturing and reduce reliance on foreign supply chains.
The Department of Energy (DOE) has a massive task ahead as it works to secure the US bulk-power system and implement the directives of Executive Order 14420. DOE will need to collaborate closely with industry stakeholders to develop clear guidelines, enforce compliance, and maintain grid reliability during the transition. By prioritizing these efforts, the DOE can build a resilient, self-reliant energy infrastructure that safeguards national security and supports the country’s long-term energy independence.

Maria Guerra
Senior Editor-Battery Technology, Informa Markets
Maria L. Guerra is a Senior Editor at
Battery Technology
, blending her engineering background with a passion for technology journalism. She holds a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Universidad Metropolitana in Caracas, Venezuela, and a Master of Science in Electrical Engineering from NYU Tandon School of Engineering.
Guerra's career spans power systems engineering, oil & gas consulting, and technical writing and editing. She worked for several years at Kellogg, Brown & Root Ltd. (KBR) in the UK, conducting power system studies and providing technical support for offshore and onshore projects. During her internship at Pequiven S.A. in Venezuela, she trained neural networks using MATLAB (Kohonen Map) to estimate electrical circuit variables for oil wells (e.g., voltage, current, and power).
In addition to her engineering roles, Guerra worked as a freelance technical editor, refining complex technical content for clarity and accuracy. She later became a Power/Analog Editor at

Battery Technology
, Guerra now delivers in-depth coverage of battery manufacturing, EV advancements, energy storage systems, and the evolving landscape of critical minerals and second-life batteries. She is passionate about uncovering the stories that shape the future of electrification, from cutting-edge battery innovations to policy shifts driving sustainable energy.
Guerra is also a member of

that a new “lightweight” variant of the tri-motor EV would go on sale on September 9.
Denza launched the new Denza Z9 GT e3 Flash Charge Premium Edition on Wednesday, as a more affordable option to the range-topping e3 Performance model.
Like the Performance version, the new Premium trim is based on BYD’s e3 platform. The setup uses three electric motors: one 230 kW (308 hp) motor up front and two 310 kW (415 hp) motors in the rear, delivering a combined 770 kW (1,032 hp) and 1,210 Nm (892 lb-ft) of torque.
Denza said the tri-motor setup enables it to accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h (0 to 62 mph) in just 2.8 seconds.

Denza Z9 GT prices by trim in China (Source: Denza)

It also has BYD’s Flash Charging technology, which lets it charge from 10% to 70% in 5 minutes. A full charge (10% to 97%) takes just 9 minutes.

Whether or not BYD will launch the new Denza Z9 GT EV Premium model overseas has yet to be confirmed.

title: Data confirms Autopilot/FSD was active in crash that killed a mother, passerby saved her baby
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Tesla Full self-Driving
Fred Lambert
| Sep 9 2026 - 7:12 am PT
A 2021 Tesla Model Y left an Alabama highway, hit two trees, and caught fire, killing its driver, 29-year-old Kayleigh Page. Her 7-month-old daughter was pulled from the burning car by a stranger who saw it happen.
Troopers reported it as a single-vehicle wreck. What they didn’t say, and likely didn’t know, is that Tesla’s own data shows the car’s driver-assist system was engaged. This is part of an
ongoing Electrek investigation
matching reported crashes to Tesla’s redacted NHTSA data.
What happened on Highway 157
Around 7:40 p.m. on Sunday, December 7, 2025, a 2021 Tesla Model Y Long Range was heading along Alabama Highway 157 near the Cullman County line, about a mile north of Battleground in Morgan County. The car left the roadway, struck two trees, and caught fire, according to the Alabama Law Enforcement Agency.
The driver,
Kayleigh Page, 29
, of Waterloo, was pronounced dead at the scene. Her infant daughter, a passenger, was hurt but survived, and a passerby who witnessed the crash rescued the baby from the vehicle, Morgan County Sheriff Ron Puckett said. The child was hospitalized in stable condition.
State troopers worked it as a routine fatal wreck. No report mentioned Autopilot, “Full Self-Driving,” or any driver-assist system. To the public, it was a car that ran off the road.
What Tesla told the federal government
Under a NHTSA Standing General Order, automakers must report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact. Tesla filed one on this crash.
In it, Tesla identifies the car as a 2021 Model Y and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as
“Verified Engaged”
— meaning it confirmed through its own telematics that the system was active. It logs a pre-crash speed of
and records a fatality. It says it holds the
event-data recorder and telematics
Then it redacts the three fields that would explain the crash: the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating area. All blacked out as “confidential business information,” the
same redactions Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports
. It even left the “crash with” and roadway fields marked “unknown,” so its own filing doesn’t say the car hit trees.
A road departure, the most common Tesla driver-assist crash
This is the failure mode that shows up more than any other. Electrek’s analysis of the full NHTSA dataset found that of the Tesla driver-assist crashes where the pre-crash movement is disclosed,
the single largest category is the car leaving its lane or the road,
well ahead of rear-ends or turns. A Tesla drifting off a highway and into the trees is not an outlier in this data. It’s the pattern.
We can’t say whether this was basic Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving,” because Tesla redacted the software version. On a rural two-lane highway at 55 mph, either could have been engaged. Basic Autopilot holds a lane and a speed on roads like this, and FSD does too. Both have documented failures where the car wandered out of its lane. The field that would tell us which system was steering is the one Tesla blacked out.
Why we keep doing this
Tesla is, more aggressively than ever, encouraging owners to treat a Level 2 driver-assistance system as if it drives itself. It sells the software as “Full Self-Driving,” Elon Musk keeps promising unsupervised autonomy is months away, and the branding invites drivers to trust the car.
Around the time of the crash, Musk even suggested that Tesla drivers could look at their phones when using FSD.
But it is still Level 2. The human is driving and responsible at all times, and Tesla’s own actions confirm it: consumer FSD still requires supervision, and its robotaxi service is a small, closely monitored fleet. That gap between the marketing and the machine breeds the complacency that gets people killed.
The redaction makes it worse. At the moment Tesla is telling owners to trust the car, it’s hiding the records that would show how the system behaves when things go wrong. What’s confirmed here is narrow and real: a driver-assist system was engaged when this car left the road and a young mother died. Everything that would explain how, Tesla sealed.
How we matched it:
the NHTSA record is unredacted on location (Vinemont/Morgan County), state, vehicle (2021 Model Y), the fatality, and the month. Tesla logs the incident time as 02:09 UTC, which converts to about 8:09 p.m. local, inside the window troopers reported, who put the crash between roughly 7:40 and 8:46 p.m. It’s the only fatal Tesla crash in that area that month. It’s the same crash. Electrek has reached out to the Alabama Law Enforcement Agency for the crash report and the vehicle data, and asked whether investigators received Tesla’s raw telemetry or only Tesla’s own interpretation of it.

title: RGNT’s 85 MPH retro electric motorcycle just got a scrambler makeover
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Sep 9 2026 - 2:42 am PT
Swedish electric motorcycle maker RGNT has expanded its lineup with a new scrambler version of its retro-inspired electric motorcycle, adding a bit more off-road attitude without messing too much with the formula underneath.
The new RGNT Street Scrambler joins the existing
Street Classic
, a model we’ve been covering since it was first unveiled
over six years ago
. The two share essentially the same electric drivetrain and battery options, but the new Scrambler model gets several changes aimed at riders who occasionally want to leave the pavement behind.
The most obvious differences are the Scrambler’s 18-inch front wheel, up from the Classic’s 17-incher, along with chunkier 18 x 2.5-inch on/off-road rubber up front. The rear remains a fat 17 x 3-inch tire. The Scrambler also gets a raised and wider handlebar, while the ride height increases by 20mm. Ground clearance rises from 230mm to 260mm, and seat height increases from 810mm to 830mm.
Those aren’t exactly Dakar Rally modifications, but they should make the bike considerably happier on gravel roads and light trails while maintaining the classic motorcycle proportions that make RGNT’s bikes stand out.
Underneath, things are familiar. Both versions use RGNT’s 46 kW direct-drive rear hub motor producing a claimed 540 Nm of peak torque. Top speed is 135 km/h (84 mph), while 0-100 km/h (0-62 mph) takes 3.9 seconds.
The standard 8.3 kWh battery is rated for 139 km (86 miles) of range, while an optional 10.1 kWh long-range pack stretches that figure to 170 km (106 miles). Despite its fairly accessible appearance, the battery is fixed rather than removable.
Charging is handled through a Type 2 connector common across Europe, with the standard 1.8 kW onboard charger providing a full charge in 4 hours and 35 minutes.
An optional 6 kW charger cuts that to 1 hour and 25 minutes, or around 50 minutes for a 20-80% charge. The company refers to it as nearly a “full tank” in the time it takes for a coffee stop, but that’s some mighty slow sipping. As far as motorcycle recharges go though, under an hour for most of a charge is still fairly impressive, especially for AC charging. This won’t be a touring bike any time soon, but for commuters and occasional trail riders, the recharge time is decently quick with that faster charger upgrade.
An on-board 6 kW charger offers a mostly-filled battery in under an hour – for an extra €1,895
Other modern touches hide behind the decidedly old-school styling, including ABS, traction control, regenerative braking, keyless starting, full LED lighting, and a 3-inch circular display supporting Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.
RGNT has been pursuing this combination of vintage motorcycle design and modern electric drivetrain technology for several years now. Founded in Sweden, the company builds its motorcycles in Gothenburg, leaning heavily into a handcrafted, small-production approach rather than trying to compete with mass-market motorcycle manufacturers on volume. Earlier this year, the company announced that it had over 600 motorcycles on European streets.
That handcrafted approach isn’t cheap, but the bikes also aren’t offensively expensive, either. The Street Classic
starts at €8,995
, while the new Street Scrambler starts at €9,495. Buyers can reserve a build with a €100 deposit, with options including the larger battery, faster charger, heated grips, luggage rack, windscreen, and side bag system.
For an extra €500 over the Classic, the Scrambler seems like an interesting way to add some dirt-road capability without losing the handsome retro styling that is arguably RGNT’s biggest calling card.
The bikes are currently only available in Europe, but RGNT has announced that it expects to enter the US market in 2027 with prices starting at US $9,995, meaning there could be RGNT Street Scramblers cruising around US streets sooner rather than later.

title: New electrode design increases battery energy density by up to 15% - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Fraunhofer ISE and its partners have developed thicker electrodes that could increase battery cell energy density by 10% to 15% without adding weight. The PFAS-free, solvent-free concept has been demonstrated in lithium-ion, sodium-ion, and zinc-ion cells and is designed for cost-effective mass production.
Lior Kahana
09 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Batteries
Energy Storage
The pouch cell
A consortium led by Germany’s
Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE)
has developed thicker battery electrodes that could increase cell-level energy density by 10% to 15% without adding weight.
The researchers demonstrated the concept in lithium-ion, sodium-ion, and zinc-ion cells. They also manufactured lithium-ion pouch-cell prototypes.
“The new cell architecture was developed with future mass production in mind: A potential electrode production line exhibits significantly lower process complexity compared to a state-of-the-art wet-coating system,” Fraunhofer ISE said in a statement. “As a result, capital costs are significantly lower. Operating costs are also lower because it requires less space and energy. This technology thus opens up the possibility, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises, to establish their own battery cell production facilities in Germany.”
Oliver Fitz, group leader for battery cell technology at Fraunhofer ISE, said the researchers increased electrode coating thickness from the conventional range of 100 µm to 200 µm to as much as 800 µm. The thicker electrodes reduce the number of current collectors required inside a cell, leaving more space and weight for active energy-storing material.
The resulting battery cells are also PFAS-free and are manufactured without toxic solvents. PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, are a large group of synthetic chemicals that are highly persistent in the environment and are often referred to as “forever chemicals.”
The research team developed the electrode and cell design as part of three projects: “VORAN – Innovative Sodium-Ion Battery Storage for Stationary and Mobile Applications,” “INFAB – Zinc-Ion Batteries for Stationary Energy Storage – Manufacturing and Assembly,” and “WinZIB2 – Globally Deployable, Innovative Zinc-Ion Battery System.”
Project partners include
Acp systems
, Helmut Hechinger, the
University of Stuttgart
‘s Institute for Photovoltaics (ipv), and the
Karlsruhe Institute of Technology/Helmholtz Institute Ulm
“In a climate-neutral energy system with fluctuating energy sources like solar and wind, stationary battery storage is an integral component for covering morning and evening electricity peaks,” said Andreas Bett, director of Fraunhofer ISE. “Germany would be well advised to build up manufacturing capacity to meet the growing demand for batteries and thereby create value within the country. If we can contribute to that, we’d be very happy.”

title: Africa’s solar panel manufacturing capacity to reach 3.5 GW this year - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Report from Ember and Africa Tech Futures Lab says solar panel manufacturing output will reach around 3.5 GW in 2026, led by new plants in Egypt and Tanzania that are geared predominantly towards US export.
Patrick Jowett
09 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Research & Development
Highlights
Manufacturing
Africa’s solar panel manufacturing capacity is set to increase to quadruple this year, according to a new report from thinktank Ember.
latest report
, developed in collaboration with Africa Tech Futures Lab, says solar panel manufacturing output will quadruple as 2 GW of manufacturing plants in Egypt and around 500 MW in Tanzania come online. Panel manufacturing capacity across a further six countries – Morocco, South Africa, Algeria, Tunisia, Nigeria and Kenya – is expected to reach around 1 GW.
The report points out that data for assessing solar panel manufacturing capacity in Africa is extremely limited, with little publicly-available documentation.
Dave Jones, Ember chief analyst and co-author of the report, told
pv magazine
that Africa’s large-scale solar manufacturing factories in Egypt, Ethiopia and Tanzania are likely trying to keep a low profile to avoid unwanted attention from the US authorities, who are aiming to reduce solar imports into the country.
“However, many smaller solar manufacturing plants across Africa are increasing capacity, and although companies are keen to make press announcements, these announcements offer very little detail on manufacturing line capacity and even less on actual manufacturing volume,” he added.
The report adds that the new panel manufacturing capacity in Egypt and Tanzania is predominantly geared toward export to the US, where prices are much higher for Chinese panels due to US tariffs on Chinese goods.
While the other six mentioned countries are geared more towards supporting domestic growth, the report adds that up to 94% of the panels installed in Africa today are still imported from China.
According to data from Ember’s China’s Solar PV Export Explorer, China imported 19 GW of PV cells and 9 GW of PV wafers into Africa in the the 2.5 years to June 2026. Over the same time period, Africa manufactured just 2.7 GW of PV panels.
“We think that, in a small part, this reflects the step-up in African solar manufacturing that will continue into late 2026 and beyond. But we think the majority would not actually be imported into the country, but rather re-shipped most likely to the US,” the report says. “Customs in most African countries do not report imports of cells and wafers, so there is no data there that helps to clarify.”
Upcoming changes to US tariffs, which are set to make imports of PV cells and panels more expensive from December this year, could reduce the ability of African nations to sell cells and panels into the US. The tariff changes follows China’s removal of its 9% export VAT earlier this year.
“This could mean solar panels end up being used domestically,” the report continues. “This would replace Chinese imports and ultimately mean Africa becomes more directly self-sufficient.”
Jones also told
pv magazine
that Chinese solar panels remain the biggest barrier to building solar supply chains in Africa.
“[Chinese panels] are extremely high quality and, at $80 or so a panel, fall into the ‘ridiculously cheap’ category,” he explained. “Africa imported just $2.4 billion of solar panels in the last 12 months, so the import bill is not big, and the value-add that countries can achieve will be small, so when countries consider solar, they need to do it in a cheap and long-term way.”
Jones added the complimenting clean technologies justify more urgency in terms of supply chains. The report highlights that Africa is already importing more dollars of batteries than solar panels from China, while Jones said that EVs, grid tech and wind turbines are also rising.
“African countries should be developing an overall cleantech industrial supply chain that seeks to leapfrog the old energy world of ‘import oil and gas, import cars, import power plants’,” Jones said.
Additional headline figures from the report indicate that a record 17 GW of solar will be installed in Africa this year, equivalent to around 100,000 solar panels a day, with a total 36 of Africa’s 54 countries on track to install a record amount of solar in 2026.
The report adds that three quarters of Africa’s solar growth is distributed solar, made up of small-scale customer-side PV systems installed mostly on rooftops. Of the estimated 26 GW of solar added in Africa between 2023 and 2025, the report says distributed solar accounted for 20 GW.

title: Sungrow turns to Samsung SDI battery cells to sustain its energy storage business - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
ungrow plans to procure Samsung SDI battery cells for its energy storage systems, primarily to support continued deliveries to the U.S. market amid tightening restrictions on China-linked supply chains.
The potential three-year, multi-GWh LFP deal could leverage Samsung SDI’s expanding U.S. production footprint, although procurement volumes, manufacturing locations and commercial terms remain undisclosed.
Vincent Shaw
09 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
Chinese inverter and energy storage supplier Sungrow plans to procure battery cells from South Korea’s Samsung SDI for use in its energy storage systems, primarily to support deliveries to the U.S. market, a person familiar with the matter told
ESS News
The source confirmed that Sungrow and Samsung SDI are moving forward with the cooperation, but declined to disclose the expected procurement volume, contract value, supply schedule or other commercial terms.
Sungrow and Samsung SDI did not respond to this publication’s requests for comment by the time of writing.
The confirmation follows reports in South Korea that Samsung SDI is negotiating a major lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery supply agreement with a global energy storage system supplier.
South Korean electronics industry outlet
The Elec
reported earlier this month that the proposed agreement would run for three years, with annual supplies amounting to several gigawatt-hours and a total contract value in the trillions of Korean won. The report did not identify the customer.
The person familiar with the matter confirmed to
ESS News
that Sungrow is the company involved and said the battery cells would be incorporated into Sungrow’s own energy storage systems. The main purpose of the arrangement is to help the company maintain its ability to supply the U.S. storage market, the source said.
While a logical outcome of the deal suited to both supplier and offtaker, it remains yet to be confirmed that Samsung SDI would supply Sungrow from its US-based cell manufacturing plants.
Samsung SDI has been expanding its U.S. energy storage manufacturing footprint through StarPlus Energy, its joint venture with Stellantis in Indiana. The Korean battery manufacturer has been converting part of the facility’s electric vehicle battery production capacity to stationary storage and said it plans to begin mass production of prismatic LFP batteries there in the fourth quarter of 2026.
LG did similar with its own JV with Stellantis
The move comes as battery and storage suppliers are adapting their supply chains to tightening U.S. restrictions on China-linked battery components and equipment.
In March, Samsung SDI also signed a three-year agreement to procure KRW 1.6 trillion ($1.1 billion) of LFP cathode materials from South Korean materials supplier L&F starting in 2027. Samsung SDI said the materials would be used to manufacture ESS batteries at StarPlus Energy as part of efforts to establish a supply chain less dependent on China for the North American market.
Sungrow and Samsung SDI have an established history in energy storage. The companies agreed in 2014 to form a joint venture targeting the Chinese ESS market, and in 2016 launched a storage manufacturing operation in Hefei, Anhui province, combining Samsung SDI batteries with Sungrow power conversion and energy management technology.
The renewed cooperation comes at a more complicated point for Sungrow’s U.S. business. The company has stated publicly that it has no current plan to establish manufacturing operations in the United States, while indicating that it is seeking greater cooperation with overseas companies in areas including components and services as it adjusts to changes in the U.S. market.
Using cells manufactured by a non-Chinese supplier in the United States could help Sungrow diversify its battery supply chain for American projects. However, the structure of the future supply chain, including where complete battery energy storage systems will be assembled and how they will comply with evolving U.S. rules governing foreign-produced grid equipment, remains unclear.

title: Switzerland's largest battery storage facility goes online - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Switzerland’s largest battery storage facility has begun operations in Gurtnellen, combining 50 MW and 8.4 MW systems developed by Axpo and Energie Uri. The Fluence-supplied project will support grid flexibility.
Sandra Enkhardt
09 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Energy Storage
Switzerland’s largest battery storage facility to date was inaugurated on Wednesday in Plattischachen, in the municipality of Gurtnellen in the canton of Uri. Axpo and Energie Uri, the two energy companies behind the project, announced the start of operations.
The project comprises two battery energy storage systems built in close proximity. Axpo’s system has a power capacity of 50 MW, while Energie Uri’s system has a capacity of 8.4 MW.
When construction began just under a year ago, Axpo said its facility would provide two hours of storage. Fluence supplied the battery systems. Axpo did not initially disclose the investment amount. A response to an inquiry from
pv magazine
was pending at the time of publication.
“Such projects also bring technological know-how to the canton, generate contracts for local companies in Uri, and secure jobs in the region. Uri benefits from this in ways that go beyond just energy supply,” said Hermann Epp, a member of the cantonal government and director of construction for the canton of Uri.
Epp said the two large-scale storage systems have transformed the industrial area into an “energy hub of national importance” and demonstrate how the energy transition can be implemented in practice.
The batteries are designed to temporarily store surplus electricity, including generation from solar and wind facilities, and feed it back into the grid when needed. According to the companies, Axpo’s system will primarily serve the national market, while Energie Uri’s system will be operated with a focus on the canton’s needs.
Axpo is expanding its battery storage portfolio across Europe. The company already operates facilities in Switzerland and Sweden, while additional battery storage projects with a combined power capacity of more than 300 MW are under construction in France, Germany, Italy, Poland and Romania.
The Swiss energy company is also increasingly developing battery storage in combination with solar and wind generation.

title: From more than 50 GW to under 10 GW: Ukraine doesn’t need its old energy system back - pv magazine Global
content: When a train comes to a halt because of an air-raid alert and you suddenly find yourself wondering how safe the next few hours will be, many of the issues we discuss in the abstract back in Germany take on a different meaning. From Aug. 18 to 20, 2026, I joined a German green-tech business delegation visiting Kyiv and Lviv. The delegation was led by Federal Minister Carsten Schneider and Sören Bartol, Parliamentary State Secretary at the Federal Ministry for Housing, Urban Development and Building. BSW-Solar was represented by President Jörg Ebel, also representing IBC Solar; Olga Kovalchuk of Goldbeck Solar; and me, representing PMT. We met with representatives of the Ukrainian government, municipalities, businesses, and project partners. On the first day alone, there were six air-raid alerts. What has stayed with me most from those three days is not any particular meeting, but the coexistence of war and the future. On the one hand, there are air-raid alerts, destroyed infrastructure, and people for whom uncertainty has become part of daily life. On the other, investments, new projects, and energy supplies for the coming decades are being planned. Ukraine is not waiting for the war to end before beginning reconstruction. It is rebuilding now. From more than 50 GW to under 10 GW The conversation with Denys Shmyhal, Ukraine’s First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Energy, was particularly striking. He illustrated the scale of the destruction with a figure that is hard to forget: before Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine had more than 50 GW of generation capacity. Following massive attacks on its energy infrastructure last winter, at times barely 10 GW remained available. Destroyed or damaged facilities, occupied sites, and severed grid connections created an enormous shortfall in a very short period of time. Such figures can seem abstract until you walk through the streets. Following attacks, and particularly during the colder months, backup generators often run continuously. They stand outside shops, apartment buildings, restaurants, and other facilities; in some places, it feels as though there is one on every street corner. They provide electricity for lighting, communications, heating, and other essential needs. But they are also noisy, burn diesel, and expose people to exhaust fumes. Some of the people we spoke with described the constant noise and smell as even more psychologically draining than the frequent air-raid sirens, precisely because the strain can persist for hours or even days. Ukraine’s strategic goal is therefore ambitious. The country wants to restore generation capacity to more than 50 GW as quickly as possible, but with a different energy mix. Discussions with the Ministry of Energy outlined a target model comprising around 30% renewable energy, hydrogen-ready gas-fired power plants, and nuclear power. By contrast, there are no plans for any significant rebuilding of coal-fired generation. From a German perspective, one does not have to agree with every element of this strategy to understand its central message: Ukraine does not want to recreate its old energy system. The priorities are speed, resilience, and greater energy independence. Resilience is not an abstract concept That is precisely why this trip changed the way I view decentralized solar and battery storage. In Germany, we often discuss economic viability, grid integration, and the levelized cost of electricity. In Ukraine, another dimension comes into play: resilience. Generating and storing electricity across many locations makes the energy system less dependent on individual large-scale power plants and long transmission lines. A solar-plus-storage system at a hospital, water utility, school, or business cannot replace the national grid. But it can keep essential services running when the grid goes down. In this sense, every decentralized system is more than an energy project; it is a small building block of national resilience. Current market data show how rapidly Ukraine is moving in this direction. Solar is already a success story in the country, accounting for nearly 10% of electricity generation. According to SolarPower Europe’s “European Battery Market Outlook 2026–2030,” Ukraine installed approximately 2.9 GWh of battery storage in 2025, nearly five times as much as in the previous year. That made Ukraine Europe’s fourth-largest storage market, behind only Germany, the United Kingdom, and Italy. More than 60% of the newly installed capacity consisted of decentralized systems for households, businesses, schools, hospitals, water utilities, and other critical infrastructure. Just under one-third came from large-scale battery storage systems providing flexibility and grid services. These figures do not tell an ordinary growth story. In many European countries, storage systems are installed primarily to optimize self-consumption and reduce electricity costs. In Ukraine, they are installed to keep the lights on. For me, the often-used term “peace energy” took on a very concrete meaning there. It is about energy independence, security of supply, and making critical infrastructure less vulnerable. More than a market for German technology The demand is enormous, but that does not automatically translate into a market for German products. At the German-Ukrainian Green-Tech Investment Round Table, we discussed investment, financing, and specific projects. One thing became very clear: technology alone is not enough. Companies that want to succeed in Ukraine over the long term must first listen. What solutions are actually needed? Which local partners can provide planning, installation, and maintenance? How do tenders and financing work? What requirements result from snow loads, damaged grids, limited resources, and the security situation? Given the sheer scale of Ukraine’s reconstruction needs, it would be a mistake to focus first on sales opportunities. The more important question is: Where can German expertise and technology, working with Ukrainian partners, create tangible and lasting value? The risks should not be underestimated, either. The German government continues to provide export credit guarantees and investment guarantees, including a special blanket guarantee for short-term export transactions with Ukraine. Coverage decisions are made on a case-by-case basis. These instruments are no substitute for thorough due diligence or strong local partners, but they can help turn initial interest into bankable projects. These images are hard to forget I grew up in peace in Germany. Until this trip, I had never visited a country at war. Visiting the Ubroken rehabilitation center in Lviv was therefore one of the most moving experiences of my life. Seeing so many people who had lost arms or legs, and who will live with these injuries for the rest of their lives, affected me deeply. What impressed me even more was the determination of the people we met. They are fighting their way back into everyday life, moving forward with a strength and resilience that are difficult to put into words. I felt deep compassion, but above all, immense respect. Behind every injury is a person whose life has been changed forever by this war. I was also deeply affected by the thousands of photographs of fallen soldiers displayed throughout the cities. Each photograph represents a person, a life, a family, and loved ones who must live with the loss. These images stayed with me throughout the journey and remain with me today. This war is not an abstract geopolitical conflict. It destroys lives, families, and futures. Every death and every injury is one too many. This senseless war must end. Now is the time for the solar industry to build relationships My most important conclusion for German solar companies is therefore clear: We should engage with Ukraine in a structured way now, rather than waiting for reconstruction projects to appear on tender portals as supposedly safe new business opportunities. Partnerships, market knowledge, and trust cannot be built with the first order. This is about more than business. Rebuilding Ukraine’s energy system is a European task. Every municipality that becomes more resilient, every company that gains greater energy independence, and every piece of critical infrastructure that is better protected strengthens not only Ukraine, but Europe as a whole. The trip showed me the immense need for new infrastructure. But I was even more impressed by the determination of people, companies, and institutions to shape that future today. For our industry, this brings both responsibility and opportunity: not simply to rebuild the old energy system, but to work with Ukrainian partners to create one that is more decentralized, independent, and resilient. Perhaps we should also turn the question around: What can Germany learn from Ukraine? We need an affordable and economically viable energy system, and renewable energy provides an essential foundation. But the cost of a kilowatt-hour cannot be the only criterion. An energy system fit for the future must also be secure, resilient, and capable of functioning in a crisis. One promising approach is a cellular energy system. Numerous local energy cells and energy islands generate and store electricity close to where it is needed. Under normal conditions, they operate as part of an interconnected grid. During an outage, however, individual cells can disconnect and continue supplying critical loads where the necessary technical infrastructure is in place. It is this combination of a strong interconnected grid and decentralized autonomy that can provide greater resilience. The energy transition is therefore about more than climate protection and affordable electricity. It is also a question of security and infrastructure policy – and it has the potential to become a source of “peace energy.” Decentralized, clean energy can reduce dependencies, strengthen security of supply, and create a foundation for more resilient partnerships. As a solar industry, our task should not simply be to install more systems. We should help build a new energy system – for Ukraine, for Germany, and for a world that needs its energy supply to become cleaner, more independent, more resilient, and more secure. Author: Felix Bräuer Felix Bräuer is CEO of Premium Mounting Technologies (PMT) and a LinkedIn Top Voice. In August 2026, he joined a German green-tech business delegation to Kyiv and Lviv.
