title: EU policymakers look to raise IAA Made in Europe threshold to 50% - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
The EU’s rapporteurs on the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act are also calling for increased EU content in solar panels and for stricter component requirements against circumvention.
Patrick Jowett
09 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Manufacturing
EU policymakers responsible for drafting a report on the European Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) have set out measures for boosting Europe’s manufacturing sectors.
Plans for the IAA were
first unveiled in March
this year. At the time, proposals included introducing EU-made content requirements for products benefiting from public funds, including solar PV and battery energy storage systems (BESS).
Since then, three Members of European Parliament – Renew Europe’s Christophe Grudler, S&D’s Pierre Jouvet, and the Green’s Anna Cavazzini – have been tasked with developing a draft report on the IAA, which is due for publication this week.
According to an update posted by centre-right party Renew Europe earlier this week, key measures of their draft review include raising the threshold for Made in Europe and low-carbon products in strategic sectors to 50% by 2036, ensuring that public funds support domestic industries and sustainability.
It also commits to increasing EU content in net-zero technologies, such as solar panels, heat pumps, wind turbines and nuclear power plants.
Renew’s update adds that clearer safeguards, including stricter definitions and component requirements, should be introduced in order to “close the door on circumvention and guarantee public funds truly benefit European industries”.
“When member states put more than €2,500 billion of public money on the table every year, through public procurement and state aid, while at the same time letting one billion euros a day flow to China, something is going terribly wrong,” Jouvet said. “European citizens are entitled to expect that part of that money goes to companies that pay wages, train European workers including young people and invest in the green transition close to where they live.”
Grudler added that the draft report proposes “simple, clear and applicable rules, without unnecessary administrative burdens for businesses and local authorities.”
“Facing fierce global competition, we must build and consolidate the value chains of our strategic sectors in Europe: from steel and aluminium to the automotive industry and clean technologies,” he added.

title: France’s installed PV capacity hits 34 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
France connected 3 GW of new solar capacity in the first half of 2026, slightly above the 2.9 GW deployed in the same period of 2025. Large-scale installations above 500 kW accounted for 28% of newly connected capacity, despite representing just 0.3% of new connections. Systems below 9 kW dominated installation numbers, accounting for 78% of new connections but only 8% of added capacity.
Gwénaëlle Deboutte
09 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Highlights
According to the latest solar energy dashboard published by France’s Ministry in charge of Energy (SDES), 3 GW of new solar capacity was connected in the first half of 2026, slightly above the 2.9 GW added during the same period in 2025.
Installations larger than 500 kW accounted for 28% of newly connected capacity but just 0.3% of new connections. By contrast, systems below 9 kW represented 78% of new installations but only 8% of newly added capacity.
As of June 30, 2026, France’s cumulative installed PV capacity stood at 34 GW, including 33 GW in mainland France and 1 GW in the overseas territories.
In the second quarter of 2026, gross solar power generation in mainland France reached 14.1 TWh, up 18% from 11.9 TWh a year earlier. Excluding self-consumption, solar generation totaled 13.7 TWh and covered 8.6% of mainland France’s electricity consumption during the period, up 1.6 percentage points from the second quarter of 2025.
35.9 GW of projects awaiting connection
The capacity of projects in the grid connection queue stood at 35.9 GW, down 1% from the fourth quarter of 2025. Of this total, 8.4 GW had already secured signed connection agreements.
The figures reflect connection requests submitted to grid operators and do not necessarily represent capacity that will ultimately be commissioned. The project attrition rate before completion remains significant and will depend, in particular, on the volumes supported by the French government in the coming years.
Nouvelle-Aquitaine, Occitanie and Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes together accounted for 50% of France’s installed solar capacity as of June 30, 2026. The three regions also represented 45% of the new capacity commissioned during the first six months of the year.
Self-consumption reaches 62% of installations
In the second quarter of 2026, 62% of PV installations generated electricity that was either fully or partially self-consumed. These systems accounted for 19% of installed capacity, unchanged from the previous quarter.
Producers in mainland France self-consumed 1,047 GWh during the quarter, equivalent to 7% of gross solar generation. Systems dedicated entirely to self-consumption generated 515 GWh, or 49% of all self-consumed solar electricity.
Fully self-consuming systems accounted for 14% of mainland installations with full or partial self-consumption and 9% of the country’s total PV fleet.

title: Italian solar redrew the day, but gas still sets the price - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Solar growth softened Italy’s midday power squeeze in summer 2026, but higher heat-driven demand and weaker hydro and wind left gas to cover most of the 7.9 TWh supply gap. The result was a sharper evening exposure: gas generation surged, prices rose most after sunset, and solar-heavy southern zones increasingly faced midday oversupply and weaker capture rates.
09 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
A PV system serving an energy community in Italy
The Italian summer changed the shape of the power day more than its size. Solar produced 13.8 TWh between June and August and held the middle of the day, but a hot season lifted demand by 5.2 TWh while hydro and wind fell 2.7 TWh, and gas covered most of what was left, adding 6.4 TWh and pushing its share of generation toward half. Prices split the same way, rising least in the hours solar owns and most after sundown, so the exposure that once ran across the whole day now concentrates in the evening, where gas still sets the price.
Solar added 1.1 TWh, gas 6.4
Italian solar produced 13.8 TWh over June to August, 1.1 TWh more than the same months of 2025, while gas added 6.4 TWh over the identical window, taking it to 30.4 TWh and lifting its share of Italian generation from 40.6% to 47.7%.
Change in Italian generation by fuel, June to August 2026 against 2025. Everything else covers coal, oil, geothermal, biomass, waste, pumped hydro and other, which moved a net 0.2 TWh between them. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E hourly data.
The gap covered by PV
Year on year demand lifted by 5.2 TWh, while hydro and wind gave up 2.7 TWh between them, run of river down 20.1%, reservoir down 27.0% and wind down 16.5%. The hydro loss came with exceptionally low river levels in the north, where the Po fell to a record low at the end of July and ran at under a third of its seasonal norm. That leaves a gap of 7.9 TWh to be covered. Gas met 80% of it and solar 14%, with higher net imports covering a further 8%, so gas and solar between them account for almost all of the domestic response. The demand growth was heat driven rather than structural. Across twelve Italian cities the mean summer temperature ran 1.7 C above 2025.
The gap to be covered is demand growth plus the loss of wind and hydro, hour by hour. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E hourly data.
Demand grew at least at midday, but that explains only part of it. The gap to cover was 2.8 GW at midday and 3.9 GW overnight, so the midday gap was around a third smaller. Gas answered far more unevenly, adding just 1.0 GW at midday against 3.7 GW across the evening peak and 4.2 GW overnight. Its weakest response of the day coincided with the strongest solar, which added 1.2 GW over last summer in precisely those midday hours.
What the price shape shows
The wholesale reference price for electricity (PUN) averaged €156.5 ($182.1)/MWh over the three months, €45/MWh above last summer, with every zone up between 38.0% and 44.2%. Only 66 of 2,182 priced hours cleared below €60/MWh, against €84/MWh of 2,208 last summer.
The Italian day ahead price by hour, June to August 2026 against 2025. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E hourly data.
Every hour was dearer than last summer, but the increase concentrated after sundown, at about €57/MWh across the evening peak against €32/MWh at midday. That divergence is a solar artefact, not a market judgement in the middle of the day. Matching hours on residual demand collapses the midday discount from €33/MWh to under €4/MWh, which attributes the great majority of it to solar rather than to the shape of demand, but the level does not disappear with it. Like for like across the day, Italian prices sat about €35/MWh above last summer. Solar itself captured €133.4/MWh, 36 more than a year earlier, but it lagged the rise in baseload, so its capture rate slipped 2.3 points to 85.3%.
What holding midday costs the gas fleet
Gas rose at both ends of the day and barely at midday.
Mean Italian gas fired output by hour, June to August. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E hourly data.
That same uneven response made the fleet cycling harder within the day. The 1.0 GW added at midday against 3.7 GW in the evening widened the swing between those two windows from 7.8 GW to 10.4 GW. Day by day, the distance between each day’s highest and lowest gas hour grew by 2.7 GW to reach 12.3 GW, and the widest day reached 18.0 GW. The fleet is not running less. It is moving further within the day, with output up in every one of the twenty four hours, by 0.8 GW at the shallowest.
The national picture has room to spare, the south does not
The national average conceals a wide zonal range.
Solar as a share of demand inside each Italian bidding zone, June to August. The dashed line marks parity with the zone’s own demand. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E hourly data.
In IT South, solar averaged 86.6% of the zone’s own demand across the middle of the day and reached 182% in its best single hour, while Sardinia averaged 87.7% and reached 171%, and IT North, which carries more than half of Italian demand, averaged just 32.8%.
Sicily added the most solar of any zone, 0.5 TWh for a 42.1% rise, and recorded the largest capture decline, down 4.5 points to 80.9%, level with Sardinia at the bottom of the Italian range. In absolute terms its solar still earned the most of the southern zones, €132.5/MWh against €131.3/MWh in IT South and €123.7/MWh in Sardinia, but it earned that against Italy’s highest zonal baseload of €163.7/MWh, and the gap between the two is what pulls its capture rate to the bottom.
IT South and Sardinia already generate more solar than they consume in about a quarter of their midday hours, Sicily in one in seven. Where that surplus cannot be exported the zonal price collapses to zero, as it did in thirteen hours in IT South and nine in Sardinia, while the North still cleared around €80/MWh.
Solar delivered what was forecast
If solar had been the source of this summer’s stress it would show up as output fell short of what the market expected, and it did not.
Italian solar against the published day ahead forecast, June to August 2026. Author’s aggregation from ENTSO-E hourly data.
Across the three months Italian solar came in 4.9% above the published day ahead forecast, beating it on 83 of the 91 days that carried one. Of those 91 days, midday solar came in more than 5% below forecast on four, more than 10% below on two, and more than 25% below on none, while across daylight hours, 06:00 to 19:00, the mean absolute hourly forecast error was 664 MW, or 6.2% of mean output.
What this means for the Italian market
Resource risk arrived together, and solar could not offset it. Hydro and wind gave up 2.7 TWh in the same season that demand added 5.2. Solar rose, but it clears a gigawatt in only thirteen hours of the day, so it covered 14% of a gap that ran through all twenty four hours and left most of the rest to gas.
The exposure sits in the evening rather than in the middle of the day. Midday prices rose 35.5% against 41.3% in the evening, and gas widened its own midday to evening gap from 7.8 GW to 10.4 GW as the burden shifted into those hours.
Capture erodes at zone level first, and the national average hides it. The 85.3% headline masks Sicily at 80.9%, down 4.5 points after 42.1% output growth, and IT South and Sardinia, which already generate more than their own demand in about a quarter of their midday hours. A national price curve does not reveal those zonal differences.
The level of Italian prices still appears to be set by gas. Only 66 of 2,182 priced hours cleared below €60/MWh, and every zone rose between 38.0% and 44.2%. Solar changed the distribution of Italian prices across the day this summer. It did not change what sets their level.
One caution applies throughout. The demand growth behind the gap was heat, and heat reverses. All of it came in July and August, and June demand came below last year, so if next summer is milder and hydro recovers, the 2026 figures read as a single year rather than a trend. What holds regardless is the shape. Solar serves the part of the day it generates in, and gas serves the rest.
How WSP’s Electricity Market Outlook can help
These are the types of questions assessed using WSP’s Electricity Market Outlook (EMO), which helps clients test how solar portfolios, storage assets and cross-border positions may perform under different weather, market and policy scenarios. The underlying model, PRIMES-IEM, has supported European Commission policy analysis for two decades. It runs European markets simultaneously to 2050, with cross-border flows derived by replicating the EUPHEMIA algorithm used in the EU Single Day Ahead Coupling. Output includes hourly prices, capture rates, hydro and cooling-water sensitivities, curtailment exposure and storage profitability projections at country and asset level.

title: Sodium-ion storage powers fully off-grid solar home in Germany - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
A homeowner in Augsburg has paired 270 kWh of BIWATT sodium-ion storage with 49 kWp of solar, creating a fully off-grid household energy system with local distributor SALZSTROM providing the solution.
09 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Batteries
Residential
A homeowner in Augsburg, Germany, wanted to run their house without a connection to the public grid. The system needed to cover household demand day and night using only onsite solar and battery storage.
The basement installation made battery safety an important part of the choice. The homeowner had concerns about installing a large lithium-ion battery system indoors and asked SALZSTROM, BIWATT’s local distributor, about alternatives. SALZSTROM proposed a sodium-ion solution based on BIWATT R2 batteries and H3 hybrid inverter.
The installation pairs a 49 kWp PV array with 270 kWh of storage. It uses 60 BIWATT R2 sodium-ion battery units and four 12 kW BIWATT H3 inverters, providing 48 kW of inverter power.
Safety and environmental impact were key factors in the battery choice. BIWATT’s sodium-ion chemistry offers greater thermal stability and a lower risk of thermal runaway than LFP, addressing the homeowner’s concerns about a large indoor battery installation.
Lithium extraction can involve significant water use and land disturbance. BIWATT’s sodium-ion technology instead draws on abundant sodium resources and hard carbon derived from coconut shells, offering a lower-impact materials route that fits the homeowner’s goal of creating an all-green home energy system.
Cold-weather performance was especially important for a fully off-grid home. In winter, any energy used to heat the batteries would have to come from the home’s own solar-and-storage system. BIWATT rates the R2 for operation down to -30°C without an auxiliary heating system, keeping more stored energy available for household use.
The result is a home energy system powered entirely by onsite solar and storage, giving the homeowner a safe, fully green energy solution.
The 60 R2 units are linked through BIWATT’s dynamic balancing technology to form a single 270 kWh storage network. Solar power generated during the day is stored for use at night and when PV output is low.
The completed system is designed to supply the whole home continuously without a grid connection or the need to purchase grid electricity.
The homeowner described the result, saying, “You made a dream come true.”
BIWATT launched the world’s first sodium-ion all-in-one HESS in 2023. The indoor R2 followed in 2024, the outdoor R3 in 2025, and the stackable all-in-one R5 and I3 C&I storage system in 2026.

title: US Army to bolster its obstacle breaching capability with autonomous vehicles
content: A Seattle-based company is set to boost autonomous operations in the U.S. Army. Overland AI, the leader in ground-based autonomous capabilities, has been selected by the U.S. Army’s Capability Program Executive (CPE) Mission Autonomy for the Engineer Autonomous Breaching Capability (EABC) initiative. This $20 million contract signifies a broader shift from proving that autonomy works to delivering an operational breaching package that soldiers can employ. Breaching mission can be executed most effectively with truly autonomous vehicles “A breaching mission can be executed most effectively with truly autonomous vehicles,” said Byron Boots, co-founder and chief executive officer of Overland AI. “Our proprietary software stack is the best solution for ensuring the safety of soldiers by modernizing the battlefield.” The company revealed that its Overland AI’s software stack, OverDrive, can be integrated onto any ground vehicles to make them autonomous and enable multi-robot coordination. This technology is being leveraged for complex military operations such as breaching to overcome obstacles and facilitate the safe passage of follow-on forces. With one operator to many robotic platforms, the company’s autonomous systems are designed to reduce the number of combat engineers needed to complete a breach. In doing so, we can reduce unnecessary risk to soldiers during these exceptionally hazardous missions. For operations that have historically cost many American lives, this shift has meaningful implications, according to a press release. Autonomous mission capabilities, spanning software stacks, hardware platforms CPE Mission Autonomy was established to accelerate Army acquisition of autonomous mission capabilities, spanning software stacks, hardware platforms, and modular payloads. Along with its partners and subcontractors, Overland AI is delivering the full capability, from operator to battlefield effect. Overland AI was selected for its innovative approach to autonomous breaching, honed through extensive work with warfighters across multiple combat engineer units and Department of War research labs, and more than 25 government demonstrations for DARPA, DIU, and the U.S. Army. The EABC program is designed to deliver a cohesive autonomous breaching package, and Overland AI is honored to bring this next generation capability to warfighters, as per the release. Breaching is a critical combat-engineering function. Forces may need to create passages through obstacles so that troops, vehicles and other equipment can continue advancing. Traditionally, combat engineers must operate in highly exposed environments while identifying and overcoming these obstacles. The EABC initiative seeks to change that equation by introducing autonomous systems into the process. The objective is not simply to put a vehicle under remote control. Instead, the Army is pursuing a broader autonomous capability that combines vehicles, software, sensors, control systems and mission-specific equipment into a coordinated package. That distinction is important as military organizations increasingly look at autonomy as a way to reduce human exposure to battlefield hazards. The company says its approach has been developed through work with combat engineers, military research organizations and government programs. Overland AI also says it has conducted more than 25 government demonstrations involving organizations including DARPA, the Defense Innovation Unit and the U.S. Army. This operational experience appears to have been an important factor in the company’s selection. The Overland AI contract comes as the U.S. military is accelerating the integration of artificial intelligence and autonomous systems across multiple domains. The Army has increasingly emphasized systems capable of operating with greater independence, while recent programs have explored autonomous intelligence, sensing, targeting, logistics and maneuver.

title: Scientists 3D print steel pressure vessel for nuclear reactors using three robots
content: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and industry partners are deploying advanced manufacturing technologies, such as heavy 3D printing and AI-driven automation, to repair broken US industrial supply chains. For instance, inside an advanced Tennessee facility, a giant three-armed robot called MedUSA crafted a three-by-five-foot nuclear pressure vessel by guiding molten steel into place. Nearby was a large 12-foot model of an impact limiter, made from strong plastic instead of the usual wood. These were battle tests for the future of American industry. America’s industrial sector is facing severe operational hurdles, driven by irregular supply chains and a shortage of skilled workers. These issues have created extreme delays in infrastructure sectors like hydropower, where acquiring major custom components can now take over ten years. Over 350 leaders gathered at ORNL for the Materials and Manufacturing Innovation Days. They discussed ways to speed up the adoption of advanced manufacturing technologies. The goal of M2IND was simple yet ambitious: remove the administrative and technical obstacles slowing advanced technology, and turn laboratory breakthroughs into factory-floor reality before time runs out. “We want to make sure we have input from industry to help guide our research and ensure that the work at Oak Ridge and the Manufacturing Demonstration Facility (MDF) is valuable to U.S. manufacturers and takes into account the supply chains needed to commercialize new technologies,” said MDF Director Ryan Dehoff. Fast-track advanced manufacturing The event featured two large 3D-printed nuclear energy structures. Researchers worked with the University of Maine to print a glass-fiber polymer model of an impact limiter. This massive component protects spent nuclear fuel shipping containers during transport and replaces traditional wood designs. Scientists also used a three-arm robotic system to print a steel pressure vessel with complex domed geometry. This project shows how additive manufacturing can produce large metal parts that usually face production issues. Standard reactor vessels use large-scale forging and welding, which face severe domestic capacity limits. The 3D-printed vessel served as a test case to evaluate additive manufacturing as a viable alternative. Supply chain issues Participants highlighted urgent needs for resilient supply chains, alternative materials, and faster part qualification. They also pushed to combine manufacturing with AI, robotics, and digital engineering. New partnerships were formed to quickly turn laboratory research into practical tools for manufacturers. Representatives from four Department of Energy offices and defense officials joined leaders from energy, manufacturing, and technology sectors at the event. Together, several key obstacles facing American industry were identified. These challenges include limited local capacity for large metal parts and long component lead times. ORNL formed key industrial partnerships to bring research into practical factory use. Yet, as forum participants repeatedly emphasized, printing a part is only half the battle. Getting it certified for real-world use is where momentum often dies. To bridge that gap, ORNL announced a joint research effort with Idaho National Laboratory to standardize digital qualification methods across different facilities Researchers hope to give regulators the data needed to certify 3D-printed nuclear and energy components in months rather than years. They plan to do this using real-time sensors, machine learning, and defect-tracking algorithms during the build process. With new partnerships signed with energy titans like SLB and Kairos Power, the push is clear. Urgency has replaced routine. America is racing to rebuild its domestic manufacturing core, starting right on the laboratory floor.

title: Thousands stranded as UK air traffic IT failure cancels 2,000 flights
content: Airline operations across the UK have reportedly resumed following an air traffic control failure that cancelled over 2,000 flights and left hundreds of thousands of travelers stranded at airports throughout the country. British airports restarted operations on Wednesday, September 9, after the hours-long shutdown a day earlier. London-based aviation data and analytics company, Cirium, reported that around 1,750 flights were cancelled Tuesday, September 8. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS), UK’s air traffic control body, reported that the departure disruption was caused by a “technical issue” in its flight processing system. Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester, and Birmingham experienced the most severe delays. Reports said more than 290 further flights were cancelled on Wednesday. The first day saw 30 percent of departures grounded. Cirium revealed that the figure fell to five percent the following day.Martin Rolfe, NATS CEO, apologized to the travelers affected by the reported “IT failure”. However, Yvonne Moynihan, Wizz Air UK managing director, and Neal McMahon, Ryanair COO, have both called on Rolfe to resign over the recurring technical issues. UK flights come to a haltThe issue began Tuesday following a technical problem at NATS, the company in charge of Britain’s air traffic control system. The failure led to the cancellation of more than 2,000 flights and stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers.According to the media, Ryanair was among the hardest-hit carriers. The airline said approximately 150,000 of its passengers were affected and that it canceled more than 200 flights. British Airways, meanwhile, canceled or diverted around 100 flights, affecting tens of thousands of passengers.A Ryanair passenger plane parked on the tarmac at an airport.Credit: RyanairRolfe disclosed that the organization was investigating the incident and believed the problem was different from those behind previous failures. However, while he apologized for the disruption and said that a cyberattack had been ruled out, he was summoned to meet Transport Minister Heidi Alexander on Wednesday.Alexander urged all passengers to “continue to check with airlines” to confirm if their flights were operating as scheduled. “I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job,” she said on the social media platform X. Earlier issues spark concernThe disruption has nevertheless raised fresh questions over the resilience of the UK’s air traffic infrastructure. Tuesday’s outage was not the first major technical problem to hit Britain’s air traffic network in recent years.A system failure in August 2023 caused widespread cancellations during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. It apparently cost airlines around USD 135 million (GBP 100 million). Another technical problem emerged in July 2025 when a radar-related fault disrupted flights at major airports, including Heathrow.In an interview with Reuters, Michael O’Leary, Ryanair CEO, said the outage was a repeat of the 2023 shutdown caused by a rogue flight plan. “Fire him. He’s been there since 2015. He is useless,” O’Leary said. The firm also issued a statement saying that over 65,000 of its passengers were affected by the outage. “How many more failures do passengers have to suffer before overpaid failure NATS CEO, Martin Rolfe, accepts responsibility for his repeated mismanagement and resigns,” McMahon noted. “Families traveling on holiday, people traveling for work and thousands of visitors to the UK have once again paid the price for NATS’ abhorrent failure,” he added. Moynihan also joined Ryanair in calling on Rolfe to resign. “I think in any industry, when you’ve had three failures, you need to consider that three strikes and you’re out. So I think it’s certainly something that he needs to look at,” she said. “A third time and a third excuse is not enough anymore.”Rolfe took full responsibility for the incident. He has been given one week to investigate what happened and report his findings to Alexander.

title: From space to Earth: How rockets control their return and landing
content: Most rocket launches are watched on the way up. Engines ignite, the vehicle climbs through the atmosphere, and its stages separate as it heads toward space.But for reusable rockets and spacecraft, reaching space is only one part of the mission. They must also find a way back to Earth.The return is far more complicated than simply falling from the sky. The vehicle has to reduce its speed, survive the heat of re-entry, and remain stable as it descends. Depending on its design, it may then use engines, parachutes, or wings to complete the landing. That journey begins by establishing a controlled path back toward the planet.Slowing down to return to EarthA spacecraft remains in orbit not because it has escaped Earth’s gravity, but because it is moving sideways fast enough to keep falling around the planet. To come home, it must first slow down.The spacecraft performs a deorbit burn by firing its engines against its direction of travel. This slows it enough to lower its orbit and enter the upper atmosphere, where drag further reduces its speed.Reusable rocket boosters follow a different path because they usually separate from the vehicle before reaching orbit. After separation, a booster may perform a boost-back burn to reverse part of its trajectory and head toward land. Alternatively, it can continue downrange toward a landing platform at sea.The booster then fires its engines again during its descent. These burns help control its speed and position it for the final approach.Every maneuver must be precisely timed. Even a small error in the vehicle’s angle, speed, or orientation could cause it to miss its landing zone.Surviving atmospheric re-entryEntering Earth’s atmosphere at high speed creates extreme heat. As the spacecraft strikes the air, the gas in front of it compresses rapidly and heats up. This can produce a layer of intensely hot plasma around the vehicle.Spacecraft use heat shields to survive these conditions. Capsules commonly carry ablative shields made from materials designed to char and gradually wear away. As the outer material is removed, it carries heat away and prevents the extreme temperatures from reaching the cabin.The angle of entry is also critical. A spacecraft entering too steeply could experience excessive heating and deceleration. One approaching at an angle that is too shallow could travel beyond its planned landing area or briefly skip back out of the atmosphere.The vehicle must also remain stable during this phase. Capsules adjust their orientation to produce limited lift and control their path. Reusable boosters use grid fins, which interact with the surrounding airflow to steer the descending rocket toward its target.Completing the landingOnce atmospheric drag has removed most of the spacecraft’s speed, its landing system takes over. The method used depends on the vehicle’s design and mission.Crew and cargo capsules generally deploy parachutes during the final stage of descent. The parachutes open in a sequence, gradually reducing the capsule’s speed. Some capsules splash down in the ocean and are collected by recovery teams, while others return to designated landing areas on land.Reusable boosters rely on powered landings. Grid fins guide the rocket during descent before one or more engines restart for the final landing burn. This burn rapidly reduces the booster’s speed as its landing legs deploy.Onboard computers continuously calculate the booster’s altitude, orientation, and velocity. They make rapid adjustments to engine thrust and steering, allowing the rocket to land vertically on a pad or a platform at sea.Spaceplanes use another method. After re-entry, they glide through the atmosphere using wings and aerodynamic control surfaces before landing horizontally on a runway.Returning to Earth is therefore not one action but a carefully coordinated sequence. Engines place the vehicle on the correct path, heat shields protect it during re-entry, and guidance systems control the descent. Parachutes, landing engines, or wings then complete the journey, bringing the spacecraft back to Earth intact and, in some cases, ready to fly again.Launching a rocket requires enough power to break free from the ground, but returning one demands precise control at every stage. It is this combination of speed, heat management, and split-second navigation that turns a fall from space into a safe landing.

title: Google-backed 615 MW nuclear plant set to power 500,000 homes again
content: The Trump administration is putting $1.9 billion toward restarting a nuclear plant in Iowa as the U.S. works to keep up with rising electricity needs from artificial intelligence. On Tuesday, the Department of Energy said it had finalized a loan of up to $1.9 billion to help NextEra Energy bring the Duane Arnold Energy Center back online.The 615-megawatt plant is set to restart in early 2029. It will be able to power almost 500,000 homes and support the expanding cloud and AI infrastructure in Iowa.Federal cash backs nuclear comebackDuane Arnold ran for over 45 years before closing in 2020. It was supposed to shut down later that year, but a derecho damaged the facility and forced it offline several months ahead of schedule.NextEra now plans to bring the plant back online. The federal loan will help pay for the work needed to restore the facility and add its power back to the regional grid.The Energy Department expects the project to boost electricity supplies and lower power costs. When it restarts, Duane Arnold will be Iowa’s only working nuclear power plant.Deputy Energy Secretary James Danly said the financing “marks another step in advancing America’s nuclear renaissance.”Google locks in nuclear powerGoogle is a key partner in the restart. In October 2025, Google and NextEra announced a deal where Google agreed to buy electricity from the plant through a multi-year contract.This agreement gives NextEra a steady customer for the electricity the plant will produce. For Google, it means a reliable power source for its growing cloud and AI operations in Iowa.“We expect Duane Arnold to be back online in early 2029, and the plant will provide more than 600 MW of clean, safe, “always-on” nuclear energy to the regional grid,” Google said in a blog post last year.Google also pledged an additional $7 billion investment in Iowa over two years. The spending includes new and expanded infrastructure supporting its cloud and AI businesses.AI pushes tech toward nuclearThe deal shows how tech companies are changing as AI increases electricity demand. Running advanced AI models needs big data centers, which use a lot of power.Google is far from alone in seeking nuclear generation. A Microsoft-backed project to restart Pennsylvania’s Crane Clean Energy Center, formerly known as Three Mile Island Unit 1, received a $1 billion Energy Department loan in 2025.Meta has also reached agreements supporting up to 6.6 gigawatts of new and existing nuclear capacity by 2035. Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta are all expanding data center infrastructure as AI workloads continue to grow.Washington accelerates atomic powerThe Duane Arnold financing also fits into the Trump administration’s broader nuclear strategy. President Donald Trump signed several executive orders in 2025 aimed at accelerating nuclear development in the U.S.One order directed the Energy Department to halt most previous plans for diluting and disposing of surplus plutonium. It instead called for a program to process the material and make it available to private companies.The Iowa project now adds another major nuclear investment to that push. If the restart stays on schedule, Duane Arnold will return 615 MW of generating capacity to the grid in 2029, giving Iowa a major new source of dependable electricity as demand from AI infrastructure continues climbing.

title: South Korea to build 614-petaflop supercomputer with 8,496 GPUs
content: The Ministry of Science and Information and Communications Technology (MSIT) and the Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information (KISTI) have announced that the next-generation national supercomputer will be launched by December this year. Dubbed Supercomputer No.6, the machine will be equipped with 8,496 graphics processing units (GPUs) and boast a 614 petaflops performance, likely pushing it into the Top 10 supercomputers in the world. Supercomputers are extremely fast and large computers that can carry out extremely complex mathematics to solve problems of engineering and science that regular computers cannot handle. From energy exploration to weather forecasting, space research to drug discovery, supercomputers are tasked with carrying out simulations that help us better understand these fields and help scientists make discoveries. Countries typically built these large-scale computers at their national institutes to make scientific breakthroughs and attain economic leadership, while also deploying them for national security measures. The world’s top supercomputers are listed in the TOP500, with the latest edition listing China’s LineShine and ending US dominance at the top of the list. South Korea has 15 supercomputers on the list, with KISTI’s Supercomputer No. 5 occupying the 109th spot. KISTI and MSIT aim to break into the top 10, with Supercomputer No. 6 coming this December. Supercomputer No.6KISTI’s Supercomputer No. 6 is built around NVIDIA’s GraceHopper 200 chips that integrate the central processing units (CPUs) and GPU units. The upcoming unit will feature 8,496 GPUs and 9,936 CPUs, 205 petabytes (PB) of onboard storage, and networking speeds that exceed 400 Gbps. Theoretically, Supercomputer No. 6’s computing performance is 614 petaflops, which is a huge leap when compared to its predecessor, Supercomputer No. 5, “Nurion, unveiled in 2017 with computing performance of 25.7 petaflops. Apart from a 24x increase in theoretical computing performance, the successor supercomputer will also get a 10x increase in storage and 4x faster networking speed. MSIT and KISTI signed an agreement with Hewlett-Packard Enterprise for system installation last year. Post-installation inspections began last month, and performance and stability testing is underway as South Korea looks for a December launch. Once operational, the supercomputer will enable access to massive computing resources for researchers engaged in computational science, data simulation, and AI-based scientific research. Plans include redistributing the resources across three programs: National Strategy (30 percent), R&D Innovation (55 percent), and Industrial Innovation (15 percent). Not smooth sailingThe announcement of the new supercomputer and its likely availability in the near term is great news for researchers. However, the acquisition was not this smooth sailing. Soon after the Supercomputer No. 5 was introduced in 2018, South Korean researchers began looking for its successor as early as 2021. However, the boom in generative AI, which has matured with ChatGPT and Claude, has now caused a huge surge in demand for GPUs. As prices for GPUs skyrocketed, South Korea couldn’t secure the chips at budgeted prices and had to spend 448.3 billion won (~US $334.9 million), a 53 percent jump over its initial budget of 292.9 billion won (~ US$218.8 million) to make the supercomputer a reality. “Supercomputer No. 6 is core infrastructure that will drive a major leap in scientific and technological research productivity in the AI era,” said Kim Sung-soo, Director General of the R&D Policy Bureau at the Ministry of Science and ICT in a press release. “We expect it to generate tangible outcomes that contribute to securing national strategic technologies, including K-Moonshot and the 7 Major SEEDs, as well as research innovation across industry, academia, and research institutes.”

title: New floating nuclear powerhouse aims to power 15,000 coastal homes
content: Bluecore Energy, a startup building small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs) on floating barges, announced an oversubscribed $50 million seed round led by Silverton Partners.Within just nine months of launch, Bluecore Energy has rapidly accelerated its path toward floating nuclear power by securing a port terminal, receiving its first barge, and starting construction on a test reactor. Designed specifically for commercial applications, the reactor incorporates multiple layers of protective shielding and continuous water-based cooling to ensure safe, resilient operation out at sea.The company’s founder, Kofi Asante, announced in the LinkedIn post: “Our focus is simple. Create and deliver zero-emission energy as safely and quickly as possible. Over 3 billion people live within an hour of water. We want to power them all.” Powering roughly 15,000 homesBluecore Energy emerged from stealth on 21 July with $10 million in pre-seed funding to deploy floating SMRs directly on mobile barges. The startup is the first SMR developer based inside a major U.S. shipping hub, operating directly out of its headquarters at the Port of Long Beach, California. The goal is to build a 10 MWe water-cooled reactor system using established maritime nuclear physics enclosed in steel pressure vessels and concrete shielding. The reactor will be capable of powering roughly 15,000 homes and can operate for years on a single fueling.Designed to be modular, multiple units can be chained together to scale up and deliver reliable, long-term power to major ports, utilities, AI data centers, offshore facilities, and energy-constrained coastal communities.Bluecore’s initial target is its hometown Port of Long Beach — the first American port to publicly back floating nuclear energy. “Nuclear energy at sea is not a new idea. Our opportunity is to take lessons from decades of maritime nuclear experience and combine them with modern engineering to build systems for a new generation of commercial applications,” stated Asante, who is a former Uber Freight executive.The startup has already secured and delivered its first physical barge alongside an electric test reactor to its port site. This will allow the engineering team to actively construct, test, and refine system components in real-world conditions. Alongside these hands-on development milestones, Bluecore is rapidly advancing its formal regulatory, design classification, and commercialization pathways by deepening its technical engagement with both the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the US Coast Guard.Accelerating development Its platform leverages offshore mobility to overcome land-based energy constraints. The company’s small modular reactors will be mounted on mobile barges that can be moored or anchored like offshore oil rigs. These will be connected directly to land infrastructure using high-capacity subsea power cables. Positioned out in open waters, the units naturally draw on the ocean for continuous cooling. According to TechCrunch, this seed round drew strong support from returning pre-seed backers, including Slauson & Co., Harlem Capital, and Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen. And high-profile new investors, such as Collab Capital, Kevin Hart’s HartBeat Ventures, and angel investors from Tesla, Uber, Amazon, and Google.With the new capital, Bluecore will place its first order for nuclear fuel. The primary operational challenge facing the company is navigating hardware supply chain issues. The startup, staffed by veterans from SpaceX, Rivian, and Navy submarine units, is already undergoing joint design review with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and the Coast Guard.

title: Meet Arrhenius a 60-petaflop supercomputer designed for research
content: Europe has added another powerful machine to its growing supercomputing network with the inauguration of Arrhenius, a new system in Sweden capable of more than 60 petaflops, or over 60 million billion operations per second.The supercomputer was inaugurated at Linköping University and will be available to researchers, companies and public-sector organizations across Europe. It is designed to tackle computationally intensive work ranging from climate simulations and materials research to life sciences, engineering and artificial intelligence.A 60-petaflop machine for European researchArrhenius is classified as a mid-range supercomputer, but its performance places it among the world’s most powerful machines. It ranked 42nd on the TOP500 list published in June 2026.Its computing capacity is intended for workloads that would be impractical or take considerably longer on conventional computing systems. Researchers can use it to run complex simulations, analyze large datasets, and develop compute-intensive AI applications.Potential applications include climate modeling, materials science, drug discovery, life sciences, and engineering. The system is also designed with security and data integrity in mind, allowing organizations to use it for proprietary product development and research involving sensitive personal data, according to the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking.Arrhenius is already being used by European researchers. Users gained early access through the EuroHPC AI for Science access call before the official inauguration, while broader access is now available through regular EuroHPC access calls as well as benchmark and development modes.Designed to deliver more computing for less energyRaw performance is only one measure of a modern supercomputer. The amount of electricity required to achieve that performance has become increasingly important as computing systems grow larger.According to EuroHPC, Arrhenius delivers more than 61 billion operations per watt. That placed it 24th on the Green500 list, which ranks supercomputers according to energy efficiency. The system was procured through a contract with HPE signed in July 2025, with an estimated total value of €68.5 million. Up to 35% of the cost is co-funded by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking through the Digital Europe Program, with additional contributions from the Swedish Research Council to Sweden’s National Academic Infrastructure for Supercomputing (NAISS). EuroHPC and NAISS, hosted by Linköping University, jointly manage access to the machine.Part of Europe’s push for computing sovereigntyArrhenius is more than a standalone Swedish research computer. It joins 12 supercomputers already procured by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking as Europe attempts to build computing infrastructure that it can control and access across the continent.The initiative is also expanding beyond traditional high-performance computing. EuroHPC is overseeing the implementation of 19 AI Factories and 13 AI Factory Antennas across Europe, while also developing a European quantum-computing infrastructure that will integrate quantum technologies with conventional supercomputers.The Swedish system is named after Carl Axel Arrhenius, the Swedish geologist and chemist who discovered the mineral gadolinite in 1787. Gadolinite was later found to contain several previously unknown elements belonging to the rare-earth group.For European researchers and businesses, however, the machine’s more immediate significance is its computing capacity. By making tens of petaflops of processing power accessible across borders, Arrhenius gives scientists and industry another resource for workloads that conventional computing simply cannot keep pace with.

title: Automation could enable speedy deployment for Rolls-Royce's reactors
content: ABB, a Switzerland-based engineering company, has signed a memorandum of understanding with Rolls-Royce SMR to explore technology for the latter’s standardized, factory-built small modular reactors.Developed through ABB’s UK operations in Warrington, the collaboration will assess how automation, electrification, instrumentation and communication solutions could help Rolls-Royce SMR scale its planned fleet. The effort is aimed at supporting the expansion of reliable and affordable low-carbon baseload power.Technology for factory-built reactorsThe agreement brings together solutions from ABB’s three business areas as Rolls-Royce SMR works to change how nuclear projects are delivered. Its approach involves manufacturing most of each reactor under factory conditions before transporting modules to the selected site for assembly.“Rolls-Royce SMR is transforming the way nuclear projects are delivered, to give greater cost and schedule certainty with a standardized, factory-built approach,” said Stacy O’Brien, Head of Procurement Enterprise at Rolls-Royce SMR.“ABB has a long and impressive record of delivering automation and electrification solutions to energy infrastructure projects, and this agreement brings an opportunity to consider how we can further strengthen our delivery team,” he added.470-MW reactor for one million homesThe Rolls-Royce SMR is a 470 MWe pressurized water reactor designed to power one million UK homes for 60 years. About 90 percent of the unit, which measures roughly 16 meters by 4 meters, will be manufactured in a factory.On-site work will largely involve assembling prefabricated and pre-tested modules. According to the company, this approach significantly reduces project risk and could shorten construction schedules.The UK government selected the reactor as its preferred technology for the country’s first SMR project in June 2025. Wylfa in North Wales was later named as the planned location for three units, although the site could potentially accommodate up to eight. A final investment decision is expected in 2029.Plans for a wider reactor fleetOutside the UK, Czech energy company ČEZ selected the technology in October 2024 for projects totaling up to 3 GW and acquired a 20 percent stake in Rolls-Royce SMR.The first unit is planned near the existing Temelín nuclear power station, with further projects being considered at coal-fired power plant sites.An early works agreement is advancing licensing, permitting and site-specific design activities for the planned deployment in the Czech Republic.“We are delighted to explore how we can work with Rolls-Royce SMR on its efforts to develop a global fleet of SMRs that can help expand reliable and affordable baseload power capacity to meet an increasing demand for low-carbon energy,” said Per Erik Holsten, President of ABB’s Energy Industries division. “Collaboration is also key – no single company or country alone can deliver the scale of energy expansion and energy transformation required to meet future demand. Partnerships along the energy value chain are instrumental for accelerating the commercialization of modern, advanced nuclear technologies,” he added.ABB is also working with Swedish reactor developer Blykalla on automation, electrification, digitalization and cybersecurity solutions for its lead-cooled SMR technology.

title: This soft robot expands and contracts to seem more alive
content: A small, fluffy robot that changes its entire body shape may seem more lifelike to people, according to a new study by researchers in Japan.The research team from The University of Electro-Communications (UEC) and Sony Corporation developed a spherical mobile robot called MOFU (MOrphing Fluffy Unit) to investigate how whole-body expansion and contraction affect a person’s perception of a robot’s “animacy,” the extent to which it appears alive or lifelike.The study, published in PLOS ONE, suggests that changing a robot’s overall volume could become another way for machines to communicate and express themselves without relying on faces or conventional articulated movements.A robot that changes its entire shapeMOFU uses a geometric mechanism known as a Jitterbug structure, in which multiple sections move together to alter the robot’s overall shape. A single motor-driven linear mechanism lets the robot’s height change from about 210 to 280 millimeters as it expands and contracts.It can also move using differential two-wheel drive, allowing it to travel straight or rotate. The researchers deliberately gave MOFU a soft, fluffy exterior and an abstract spherical appearance rather than making it resemble a particular animal. Direct-drive motors and other low-noise components also reduce mechanical sounds, while an internal battery lets the robot operate without a cable. The design was inspired in part by how living organisms change their overall volume. Breathing is an obvious example, but volumetric movements can also appear in animal displays, such as a frigatebird inflating its throat pouch or a peacock spreading its feathers. The researchers wanted to determine whether this type of movement could similarly make an artificial machine appear more alive.Testing whether movement makes a differenceMOFU’s expansion and contraction naturally causes some rotation around its vertical axis. To isolate the effects of each movement, the researchers used its wheels to cancel out that rotation, creating an expansion-and-contraction-only motion. They also produced rotation-only movements for comparison.The team then conducted three online video experiments with 498 participants after excluding incomplete or invalid responses. Participants watched 20-second videos of MOFU and rated its animacy using six items from the Japanese version of the Animacy subscale of the Godspeed Questionnaire Series, with each item rated on a five-point scale.In the first experiment, both expansion-contraction and rotational movement increased perceived animacy compared with conditions in which the respective movement was absent. The researchers found no clear difference between expansion-contraction-only and rotation-only conditions.A second experiment examined whether using two robots instead of one would change the effect. It found no clear difference in perceived animacy between one and two expanding and contracting MOFUs. In the two-robot tests, however, conditions involving movement generally received higher animacy ratings than completely stationary robots.The third experiment added MOFU’s expansion, contraction, and rotation to locomotion. Participants rated the moving robot as more animate than one that only traveled around. The researchers caution, however, that this experiment had fewer participants than originally planned and needs to be repeated with an adequate sample size.Making robots feel more expressiveThe findings suggest that changing a robot’s overall body volume may itself influence how alive people perceive it to be. The researchers say future experiments should compare expansion-contraction directly with other forms of robotic movement and investigate how changing the speed, amplitude, and timing of the movement affects perception.There are also limitations to the current study. Because participants watched videos online, the researchers did not examine how MOFU’s softness, sound, or physical presence might affect people’s responses. In-person studies in the future could therefore explore whether whole-body movement influences not only perceived animacy but also feelings such as comfort, warmth, eeriness, and willingness to approach.Such capabilities could eventually be useful for robots designed to interact closely with people, particularly in healthcare and welfare environments where quiet, expressive, and space-efficient machines could be valuable.

title: Hanwha unveils 50 kW laser vehicle that kills drones at $1.50 per shot
content: Hanwha is developing a 50-kilowatt laser weapon mounted on an armored vehicle, targeting militaries looking for a mobile and relatively inexpensive way to counter the growing threat from drones.The South Korean defense group unveiled the concept at MSPO 2026 in Kielce, Poland, where Hanwha Systems is showcasing its laser technology alongside a more comprehensive portfolio of air-defense and counter-unmanned systems. The company has already developed a prototype and plans to begin serial production of the laser vehicle by the end of 2027, according to company representatives speaking to Defense News.A laser on an armored 8×8The new system combines a 50 kW version of Hanwha’s Cheongwang laser technology with the company’s Tigon 8×8 armored personnel carrier. Cheongwang is South Korea’s first operational laser weapon and has been deployed since 2024 to protect strategically important locations. The new vehicle-mounted system increases the laser’s power while adding the mobility needed to keep pace with military forces and respond to moving targets.Hanwha says the system is intended to track and engage fast-moving targets, with drones being a key focus. The company is also emphasizing the economics of using directed energy against relatively inexpensive drones. According to Hanwha, a Cheongwang laser shot costs around 2,000 South Korean won, or about $1.50. Unlike conventional interceptors, a laser does not require a separate physical projectile for every engagement, which may make it attractive when forces face large numbers of low-cost drones. Hanwha Systems manager Hyungun Park told Defense News that the company is currently discussing potential Cheongwang exports with countries in Europe, Asia and the Middle East.Building a layered counter-drone networkThe 50 kW vehicle is being presented as part of a broader Hanwha approach to layered air defense rather than as a standalone weapon. At MSPO, Hanwha is displaying the H-Shield counter-drone system, a 40 mm wheeled counter-UAS platform, the H-SHORAD short-range air-defense system and the L-SAM long-range surface-to-air system. The company’s systems are designed to work through a command-and-control network, with interceptor drones also included in the architecture. The company is also displaying a 20 kW tactical laser vehicle, giving it multiple mobile directed-energy concepts alongside the larger 50 kW system.The emphasis on Poland is significant. Hanwha has built a growing defense relationship with the country, beginning with the selection of its K9 chassis for Poland’s Krab self-propelled howitzer program in 2014. Poland has since become a major customer for the K9 and Chunmoo multiple rocket launcher, known locally as Homar-K.For the new laser vehicle, mobility could be as important as raw power. Mounting the weapon on the Tigon gives the system an armored, wheeled platform that can move with ground forces rather than remaining tied to a fixed installation.Hanwha plans to continue development toward serial production by the end of 2027. Whether the system can translate its promising low-cost-per-shot economics into an effective battlefield capability will depend on factors such as detection, tracking, weather conditions, power generation, and the ability to engage multiple targets.The new prototype is another step in the growing effort to put high-power lasers on mobile military platforms, as armed forces look for more sustainable ways to deal with increasingly large numbers of drones.

title: US Navy selects VAMPIRE system to fight drones with 70mm rockets
content: L3Harris Technologies, a U.S. defense technology company, has been selected by the U.S. Navy to deliver VAMPIRE counter-unmanned systems for littoral defense, the company announced on September 8.The weapons will support the United States’ growing integrated counter-unmanned systems architecture. VAMPIRE is a self-contained system that provides advanced reconnaissance and precision-strike capabilities against drones and remotely piloted platforms across multiple operating domains.Self-contained counter-drone weaponVAMPIRE stands for Vehicle-Agnostic Modular Palletized Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Rocket Equipment. L3Harris describes it as a portable kit that can be installed on most vehicles equipped with a cargo bed.The system brings reconnaissance and precision engagement capabilities together in a single weapons solution. According to L3Harris, VAMPIRE can be configured to launch Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS) rockets or other laser-guided munitions. However, the company has not identified the ammunition that will be supplied with the Navy systems. The anti-drone system can engage targets at ranges of up to 9 miles (15 km) when equipped with laser-guided 70mm APKWS rockets.L3Harris says the wider VAMPIRE family incorporates sensors, precision weapons, electronic jammers and non-kinetic effectors. It uses artificial intelligence and machine learning to accelerate the detection, engagement and defeat of small unmanned threats.The company has developed several versions of the system for different missions. These include land, maritime, airborne, containerized, base-defense and electronic-warfare variants, although L3Harris has not specified which named variant the Navy will receive.VAMPIRE modified for maritime conditionsL3Harris is engineering new capabilities for the Navy and ruggedizing VAMPIRE against the environmental stresses encountered in maritime environments. The company did not provide technical details about those modifications.“VAMPIRE is a flexible and effective system that meets the unique requirements of the U.S. Navy for littoral C-UxS defense,” said Tony Calderon, president of Targeting & Sensor Systems within L3Harris’ Communications & Spectrum Dominance business. “We’re engineering new capabilities to adapt to our customers’ missions and ruggedizing VAMPIRE against the environmental stresses of maritime environments,” he added.The value of the Navy order was not disclosed. L3Harris also did not reveal the number of systems involved or provide a delivery schedule. The announcement did not include an engagement range, launcher capacity, or other performance specifications.Layered defense against unmanned systemsThe Navy selection follows a separate U.S. Army order for VAMPIRE. Together, the programs extend the system’s use across the two military services, although their respective configurations have not been detailed.L3Harris is separately delivering Wraith Shield software to support layered counter-drone operations. Unveiled earlier in 2026, the software provides a radio-as-a-sensor capability designed to help defeat small drones.Wraith Shield can be incorporated with VAMPIRE and the company’s Drone Guardian system. L3Harris describes Drone Guardian as a counter-unmanned aircraft system that autonomously detects, tracks, and identifies drone threats using multiple correlated sensors.Integrating the three technologies provides layered defense against unmanned threats. VAMPIRE supplies reconnaissance and precision-strike capabilities, while Wraith Shield contributes radio-based sensing and Drone Guardian adds autonomous detection, tracking, and identification.L3Harris provides defense technology across the space, air, land, sea, and cyber domains. The Navy selection adds VAMPIRE to the company’s expanding work on counter-unmanned systems for U.S. military customers.

title: JBC's B.IRON Battery-Powered Rework brings high precision to electronics repair
content: As electronics become smaller and more complex, JBC’s B.IRON Battery-Powered System is designed to be more precise, mobile, and comfortable to use. It combines cordless operation with quick heating, smart temperature control, and app-based controls for soldering and rework, all in a lightweight, ergonomic design.Among its various configurations, B.IRON Nano Rework is meant for carrying out delicate surface-mount device (SMD) repairs on densely populated printed circuit boards (PCBs), especially when working under a microscope or with tiny SMD parts.Cordless design supports precision workThanks to its battery-powered system, B.IRON removes cables and external control units. The stand’s built-in charger recharges the tool automatically whenever it’s returned to its holder. This keeps the tool ready for repeated use while giving operators unrestricted movement around the work area.The system is made for places where precise positioning is important, like research labs, electronics manufacturing, aerospace, medical devices, automotive electronics, and field service. Without cords, it is easier to reach tight spaces and crowded circuit boards.JBC tools are lightweight, weighing just 1.2 ounces (35 grams), reducing fatigue during extended use. They also feature a short tip-to-grip distance, which lets users hold their hand closer to the soldering point, improving stability and control.B.IRON reaches 350°C in under three secondsB.IRON uses JBC’s Exclusive Heating System to reach 662°F (350°C) in under three seconds and quickly recovers heat after each solder joint. This steady heat helps keep soldering quality high during long runs and detailed repair work.The system also has Intelligent Heat Management. When the tool is placed in its stand, it enters Sleep Mode and lowers the tip temperature below the solder’s melting point. If left unused longer, it switches to Hibernation Mode, cutting power to reduce oxidation and make the tip last up to 5 times longer. Once the tool is taken off the stand, the tool quickly heats back up without any manual changes.When moving around the work area, a Safety Cap activates a power-safe mode for extra protection.B.IRON Nano Rework focuses on miniature electronicsB.NANO is designed for soldering in tight spots and lab work, and can handle up to 120 small SMD solder joints on a single battery charge. B.TWEEZERS is designed for removing and replacing very small SMD parts. Its cartridge alignment system keeps the tips in the right place during rework and allows up to 60 SMD rework jobs per charge.Both tools work with C115 Cartridge Range.Live temperature, battery level, and heating curve, visible in real time B.IRON allows users to customize their station with different tools, combining them to suit their needs. Expansion kits let users add a second tool, so they can turn their current station into a dual-tool or rework setup without needing a new system.Users can set tool temperature, battery level, and other settings using B.IRON app, which is available on iOS and Android to be used on your own device. With cordless tools and modular stations, B.IRON gives electronics professionals a flexible platform for prototyping, production, and high-precision work.

title: AEON enters Humanoid Gym ahead of planned 1,000-robot deployment
content: Hexagon Robotics and motion technology company Schaeffler announced last month that AEON had entered Schaeffler’s Humanoid Gym in Germany, advancing a collaboration to bring humanoid robots into industry.The facility will be used to teach AEON new manufacturing capabilities, validate what it learns, and prepare the robot for deployment. The partners are working towards the planned deployment of at least 1,000 AEON humanoids over the coming years.By placing the robot inside an industrial training environment, the companies can develop its abilities while Schaeffler builds the knowledge required to introduce humanoids into its operations.A three-stage route to industrial deploymentThe Humanoid Gym is organized around a train–validate–deploy model. Each capability is first taught to AEON, then assessed before the robot is prepared to apply it in an industrial setting.This structure gives the companies a defined process for moving capabilities from training into practical deployment. It creates a dedicated space where the robot can be prepared for manufacturing work as the partnership develops.The facility has a second purpose. Schaeffler will use the program to develop its expertise in operating, training, and integrating humanoid robots.Those three areas address different parts of adoption. AEON needs to acquire the required industrial capabilities, while Schaeffler’s teams need the knowledge to manage the robot and incorporate it into the company’s manufacturing environment.The gym therefore supports the development of both the technology and the organisation expected to use it. This combined focus prepares AEON for work beyond the training facility.Collaboration moves towards 1,000-robot planAEON’s arrival at the Humanoid Gym marks the next stage of the strategic collaboration between Hexagon Robotics and Schaeffler. Their plan calls for the deployment of at least 1,000 humanoids, although the companies have not disclosed a timetable for individual deployments.They have also not identified which industrial capabilities AEON will learn first or the manufacturing tasks it will initially undertake. For now, the gym establishes the process through which those capabilities can be developed and checked.The planned scale means Schaeffler must prepare more than the robots themselves. It needs people with the skills to train the humanoids, oversee their operation and integrate them into industrial processes.Work inside the gym will allow that internal expertise to develop alongside AEON’s capabilities. The partners can consequently prepare for deployment through a shared program rather than treating robot training and organizational readiness as separate efforts.The milestone does not mean that the planned fleet has already entered service. Instead, it begins the industrial preparation intended to support that future deployment.Building the foundation for wider adoptionThe collaboration is intended to accelerate the adoption of next-generation automation in manufacturing. AEON’s entry into the gym gives both companies an industrial environment for the training and validation required before deployment.It also allows Schaeffler to build practical expertise before the planned number of humanoids expands. The work completed there will underpin the partners’ effort to move AEON from capability development into industrial operations over the coming years.

title: China unveils humanoid built to automate crop breeding, pollination
content: A new humanoid robot designed to support crop breeding has been unveiled in Beijing, highlighting the growing use of embodied AI in agriculture. GEAIR 2.0 was presented at the 33rd China Beijing Seed Industry Conference as a system capable of autonomously performing tasks involved in hybrid pollination. Developed by a team from the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the robot is designed to operate in complex crop environments without continuous human control. Its developers say the upgraded system improves the robot’s ability to work among leaves and branches while enhancing its flower-recognition capabilities.Robot automates pollinationGEAIR 2.0 combines robotics, artificial intelligence and biotechnology to automate hybrid pollination for crop breeding, a labor-intensive step in the process. The humanoid robot can identify flowers, navigate around plants and perform pollination autonomously, allowing it to work for extended periods without continuous human supervision.The upgraded robot uses two arms instead of the flexible single-arm system used previously. This allows it to maneuver more effectively around leaves and branches and adapt to changing conditions inside crops. Its stigma-recognition accuracy (its ability to identify a flower’s female reproductive organ) has also improved from 85 percent to 92.8 percent. During its launch in Beijing, GEAIR 2.0 demonstrated tomato pollination by using one hand to hold a pollen tube and the other to operate a pollination brush. The robot completed each pollination in less than 10 seconds, while a single dip of the brush into pollen could support about 50 pollinations, as reported by China Daily.The system’s name refers to Genome Editing combined with AI-based Robotics. Researchers use gene editing to create male-sterile plants with exposed stigmas, making the reproductive structures easier for the robot to identify and access. The approach, described as “crop-robot co-design,” was detailed in a 2025 study published in Cell. Researchers found that automated tomato cross-pollination could achieve efficiency comparable to manual methods and later extended the approach to soybean.The developers say automating pollination could reduce the need for manual labor, lower breeding costs, and improve the efficiency of hybrid breeding. Robots could also perform repetitive tasks for longer periods and operate under varying environmental conditions, potentially making them useful for large-scale crop breeding operations.AI transforms breedingIn this process, the researchers first modify the plants to expose the stigma, removing the need for workers to manually open petals and giving the robot easier access to the reproductive structure.The robot must then navigate through dense crops, avoid branches and leaves, and locate the needle-sized stigma with enough precision to complete pollination. This allows it to perform repetitive breeding tasks for longer periods than human workers, including during different times of day and under varying weather conditions, the Global Times reported.According to experts, hybrid pollination is physically demanding and must often be completed within a narrow time window. Robots could let farmers manage the process while reducing the manual labor required.Researchers describe the approach as integrating biotechnology and AI to make crop breeding more efficient and less dependent on intensive manual work. The technology could help reduce breeding costs while improving productivity and supporting large-scale hybrid crop development.The push for AI-enabled breeding is also part of China’s broader effort to modernize agriculture and strengthen food production. China’s grain output reached a record 715 million tons in 2025, while national plans call for increasing comprehensive grain production capacity to about 725 million tons by 2030. Technologies such as embodied AI could play a role in meeting those targets.

title: Anthropic researcher resigns, claims AI labs are racing toward danger
content: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from his role in pre-training AI models over safety concerns. In the X post, he claimed that the unchecked corporate race to develop AI poses an unprecedented danger to humanity.The 27-year-old pre-training researcher’s dramatic resignation has fired off a provocative warning that instantly sent ripples across the tech sector. Coxon stated that no single human activity right now poses a greater threat to civilization than the relentless corporate sprint to build “self-improving superintelligence.”“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible – but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger,” he wrote on the social media platform, X. I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below.— Jacob Coxon (@hilbertspaess) September 9, 2026The impact of AI on humans Rushing to build advanced AI without guardrails poses a danger to humanity — one that could outpace the threats of nuclear conflict and global climate change.“I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” he wrote. Coxon argued that corporate rivalry forces tech labs into a risky race to build dangerous AI systems before their competitors. To break this momentum, he urged his peers to speak out and called for a temporary ban on capability improvements to force a shift toward international coordination and safety control.“I don’t feel like we’re on track to prevent a global race, which may require costly actions such as a temporary ban on improving model capabilities,” the post added. Another Anthropic insider backed Coxon’s warnings about AI safety risks. Alignment Science Lead Evan Hubinger admitted on X that he and his colleagues fear AI could “kill all humans.” He estimates a greater than 10 percent chance of catastrophe within the decade. Hubinger acknowledged the company lacks a solution for aligning superintelligence. Anthropic is not currently on track to solve the problem.“Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” Hubinger wrote. Competitive raceDrawing from his experience at both OpenAI and Anthropic, he noted that while OpenAI staff often fail to grasp the civilizational risks, Anthropic employees understand the danger clearly. However, Coxon warned that Anthropic remains trapped in a competitive race to build superintelligence first. Gizmodo reported that the Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei shares surprisingly similar AI safety concerns with his former employee. It even gave Amodei the label of an industry “doomer” through his lengthy blog posts on the subject. This shared existential anxiety shows a striking contradiction: the head of a premier AI firm harbors deep dread about the technology he is racing to create.Reportedly, the resignation aligns with a growing push from top industry figures a deliberately slow AI scaling. In a recent “Pacing the Frontier” statement, leaders from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta acknowledged that intense competitive pressures make unilateral pauses impossible. Instead, they call for US government support and international governance to buy time for safety research. OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki warned that no lab currently has the safety capabilities required to continue scaling AI at top speed.How rapid AI scaling will actually play out and whether it poses a true existential threat — remains up for debate. What isn’t debatable is that keeping checks on AI model development has become inevitable.
